Check: you see the four directories, the five empty files, fruits.txt and numbers.txt; wc -l prints 7 and 20000. → Navigation Redirects The root of the system: save the tree of /, only one level deep, into Reports/system.txt (look in man tree for the option that limits how deep tree goes); print Reports/system.txt with cat. Check: tree printed nothing on the display, and the file shows the main directories of the system: boot, dev, etc, home, proc, tmp, usr and var; bin is a link to usr/bin. → Output Append and overwrite: save the tree of /usr, one level deep, into Reports/tree.txt; append the tree of /var, one level deep, to Reports/tree.txt, and print the file; overwrite Reports/tree.txt with the tree of /home, one level deep, and print the file again. Check: after the append, the file has both trees: /usr with bin, lib and share, then /var with cache, lib and log; after the overwrite, it has only the tree of /home, with student. → Output Errors apart: with a single ls -a command, list /etc/skel (the files copied into the home directory of every new user) and /root (the home directory of the administrator), so that the list goes into Reports/list.txt and the error into Reports/errors.txt; print the content of the two files. Check: nothing appears on the display when you run ls; Reports/list.txt has, among others, .bashrc and .bash_profile, and Reports/errors.txt has a Permission denied for /root. → Errors Append errors: run ls /root and save its error into Reports/errors.txt, overwriting the file; print /etc/shadow (the file with the passwords of the users) with cat, and append its error to Reports/errors.txt; print the content Reports/errors.txt. Check: Reports/errors.txt has two lines, one for /root and one for /etc/shadow: only root can read them. → Errors The users and the groups: copy /etc/passwd (the list of the users) into Reports/users.txt without cp: print it with cat and redirect the output into the new file; copy /etc/group (the list of the groups) into Reports/groups.txt in the same way; count the lines of the two copies and of the two originals with wc -l. Check: every copy has the same number of lines as its original. → Output Everything in one file: run ls -a /etc/skel /root so that both the list and the error go into Reports/all.txt, using &>, and print the file; run the same command again, this time with the older way, > Reports/all.txt 2>&1 (see the table of redirects), and print the file again. Check: both times, Reports/all.txt has the error for /root and the files of /etc/skel, and nothing appears on the display when you run ls. → Redirects Silence: search /etc and /usr for files called os-release with find, and throw the errors away so that you do not see any Permission denied message; print the content of /etc/os-release (the file that describes your distribution) with cat. Check: find prints only two paths, /etc/os-release and /usr/lib/os-release; /etc/os-release has the name and the version of your distribution, Fedora Linux. → Special Files Input from a file: sort /etc/shells (the list of the shells installed in the system) with sort, giving it the file with <; count the lines of /etc/passwd with wc -l, giving it the name of the file as a parameter; count them again, this time giving the file with <. Check: the shells in /bin come before the ones in /usr/bin; both counts are the same, but only the first wc prints the name of the file. → Input Type a file: run cat with a redirect, so that what you type goes into Reports/todo.txt; type three lines, then press Ctrl+D at the beginning of a new line to end the input; print the content of Reports/todo.txt. Check: cat Reports/todo.txt prints the three lines you typed. → Input Pipes: count the programs in /usr/bin with ls, wc -l and a pipe; count the files and directories in /etc (the configuration of the system) that ls shows, in the same way; show the long list of /etc (ls -l) on one screen at a time, with less. Check: there are more than a thousand programs and a few hundred entries in /etc; less stops after every screen, and you quit it with q. → Pipes Search with grep: show the line of your user, student, from /etc/passwd (the list of the users); count the lines of /etc/passwd that contain nologin: these are the users of the services, which cannot log in; list the programs in /usr/bin whose name contains zip. Check: your line ends with /home/student:/bin/bash; most of the users have nologin; the list of programs has gzip and gunzip. → Searching for a Text Repeated lines: run uniq fruits.txt and find out why it does not remove anything; print every fruit from fruits.txt only once; print every fruit with the number of times it appears, the most frequent first; print only the fruits that appear exactly once (look in man uniq). Check: uniq fruits.txt prints the same 7 lines; after sort, you get 4 fruits, 3 apple is the first line of the count, and only cherry and kiwi appear exactly once. → Repeated Lines Zeros and random bytes: show the first 16 bytes of /dev/zero in hexadecimal, with head and xxd; show the first 16 bytes of /dev/urandom in the same way, and run the command twice. Check: the bytes of /dev/zero are all zeros; the bytes of /dev/urandom are different every time you run the command. → Special Files Processes My shell: print the PID of your shell; list the processes of the terminal with all the columns of -f; show only the Name, State, Pid and PPid lines of the /proc/$$/status file of your shell: give grep every text after its own -e (grep -e Name -e State ...), and look in man grep for the option that matches only whole words, so that Pid does not also match TracerPid. Check: ps and status show the same PID and PPID for bash, and its state is S. → Listing Processes · The /proc File System Inspect a process: in the second terminal, run sleep 1000; in the first terminal, find the PID of sleep with pgrep; print its /proc/<PID>/status file; print its command line, from /proc/<PID>/cmdline, with cat -v; find out its program and its current directory, from the links /proc/<PID>/exe and /proc/<PID>/cwd; stop sleep with Ctrl+C in the second terminal. Check: the state is S, the command line is sleep^@1000^@, the program is /usr/bin/sleep, and the current directory is the one you were in when you ran sleep (run pwd in the second terminal to compare). → The /proc File System Open files: list the File Descriptor Table of your shell, from /proc/$$/fd; in the second terminal, run sleep 1000; in the first terminal, find the PID of sleep and list its File Descriptor Table; stop sleep with Ctrl+C and try to list its table again. Check: 0, 1 and 2 point to a /dev/pts/... file, a different one for each terminal (bash also keeps 255 open on the same terminal, for its own use); after Ctrl+C, /proc/<PID> no longer exists. → The /proc File System The system: Find out about your computer using only the files in /proc: the model of the processor: the model name lines of /proc/cpuinfo (use grep); how many processors you have: count the processor lines of /proc/cpuinfo; the total memory: the MemTotal line of /proc/meminfo; for how many seconds the system has been running: the first number in /proc/uptime; the version of the kernel: /proc/version. Check: the number of processors is the same as the one printed by nproc, the time matches the up part of uptime, and the version of the kernel is the same as uname -r. → The /proc File System top and htop: start top, sort the processes by memory, then by processor, and quit; start htop, search for bash and press F3 until the chosen line is the bash of the first terminal (the PID printed by echo $$), show the processes as a tree, and quit. Check: top shows the Tasks line with the number of processes in every state; in the tree of htop, your bash is under the terminal. → top · htop Archives and compression Three compressors: delete numbers.txt.gz, numbers.txt.bz2 and numbers.txt.xz, if they exist; compress numbers.txt with gzip, with bzip2 and with xz, keeping the original file every time; compare the sizes of the four files with ls -l. Check: you have numbers.txt, numbers.txt.gz, numbers.txt.bz2 and numbers.txt.xz, and the .xz file is the smallest. → Compressing One File How much smaller: delete numbers.txt.gz, numbers.txt.bz2 and numbers.txt.xz, if they exist; compress numbers.txt with gzip, with bzip2 and with xz, keeping the original file, so that each of them prints how much smaller the file got (look in their manual pages for the option that prints more details). Check: gzip and bzip2 printed how much they saved, as a percentage, and the one of bzip2 is larger; xz printed a ratio instead (about 0.045, the new size divided by the old one), so it saved about 95%, the most of the three. → Compressing One File Decompress: delete numbers.txt.gz and numbers.txt.bz2, if they exist; compress numbers.txt with gzip, without keeping the original, and check with ls that numbers.txt is gone; get numbers.txt back from numbers.txt.gz; compress numbers.txt with bzip2, keeping the original, then delete numbers.txt; get numbers.txt back from numbers.txt.bz2, this time keeping the compressed file. Check: wc -l numbers.txt prints 20000 both times; numbers.txt.gz is gone (gunzip deleted it, like gzip deletes the original), but numbers.txt.bz2 still exists. → Compressing One File What kind of file: delete numbers.txt.bz2 and numbers.txt.xz, if they exist; compress numbers.txt with bzip2 and with xz, keeping the original; find out the types of numbers.txt, numbers.txt.bz2 and numbers.txt.xz, with a single file command; delete numbers.txt.bz2 and numbers.txt.xz; find out the type of /usr/share/man/man1/ls.1.gz, the manual page of ls. Check: file says ASCII text, bzip2 compressed data and XZ compressed data, and gzip compressed data for ls.1.gz: the manual pages are stored compressed with gzip, and man decompresses them when you read them. → Which One to Use A tar archive: create Archives/music.tar with the directories Music and Photos and the file fruits.txt; list the content of the archive; find out the type of the archive with file. Check: the archive has Music/, Photos/, the five empty files and fruits.txt, and file says POSIX tar archive. → Archives Extract: create Archives/music.tar with Music, Photos and fruits.txt (if it already exists, tar overwrites it); create the directory /tmp/extract with mkdir -p, so that there is no error if it already exists; extract Archives/music.tar into /tmp/extract. Check: tree /tmp/extract shows Music, Photos and fruits.txt, with the same files as in ~/lab03. → Archives Only one file: create Archives/music.tar with Music, Photos and fruits.txt; create the directory /tmp/single with mkdir -p, so that there is no error if it already exists; extract only Photos/dog.jpg from Archives/music.tar into /tmp/single. Check: tree /tmp/single shows Photos/dog.jpg, and nothing else. → Archives Add a file: create Archives/music.tar with Music, Photos and fruits.txt; add numbers.txt to Archives/music.tar, without creating the archive again; list the archive with the details of every file. Check: numbers.txt is the last file in the list, with the size 108894. → Archives Compressed archives: create Archives/all.tar with Music, Photos and numbers.txt; create Archives/all.tar.gz, Archives/all.tar.bz2 and Archives/all.tar.xz, each with the same three entries, compressed with gzip, bzip2 and xz; compare the sizes of the four archives with ls -l. Check: the .tar is the largest and the .tar.xz the smallest. → Compressed Archives List compressed archives: create Archives/all.tar.gz, Archives/all.tar.bz2 and Archives/all.tar.xz, each with Music, Photos and numbers.txt; list the content of each archive, without telling tar how it is compressed; find out the types of the three archives with file. Check: all three lists are the same; file shows a different compression for each of them. → Compressed Archives Extract compressed archives: create Archives/all.tar.gz, Archives/all.tar.bz2 and Archives/all.tar.xz, each with Music, Photos and numbers.txt; create the directories /tmp/gz, /tmp/bz2 and /tmp/xz; extract each archive into its own directory: the .tar.gz into /tmp/gz, the .tar.bz2 into /tmp/bz2 and the .tar.xz into /tmp/xz; show the three directories with tree. Check: the trees of the three directories are the same. → Compressed Archives A zip archive: delete Archives/all.zip, if it exists (zip would update it, not create it again); create Archives/all.zip with Music, Photos and numbers.txt, with everything inside the directories; list the content of the archive; extract it into /tmp/unzipped. Check: unzip -l lists 8 entries, and tree /tmp/unzipped shows Music with three files, Photos with two files, and numbers.txt. → Zip Archives Update a zip archive: delete Archives/all.zip, if it exists; create Archives/all.zip with Music, Photos and numbers.txt, with everything inside the directories; add fruits.txt to Archives/all.zip; list the files in the archive with zip -sf; extract only fruits.txt from the archive into /tmp/fruit. Order matters: run ls /etc/skel /root > Reports/a.txt 2>&1 and print Reports/a.txt; run ls /etc/skel /root 2>&1 > Reports/b.txt and print Reports/b.txt; find out why the error is in a.txt, but not in b.txt. Check: the second command printed the error on the display, and Reports/b.txt has only the list of /etc/skel. Hint: the shell reads the redirects from left to right. → Redirects See and save: In a single command line, save the list of the programs in /usr/bin into Reports/programs.txt and count them (look in man tee for the command that writes its input both to a file and to its output). Check: the number printed is the same as wc -l < Reports/programs.txt. → Pipes Redirects seen from inside: in the second terminal, run sleep 900 < ~/lab03/fruits.txt > /tmp/out.txt 2> /dev/null; in the first terminal, find the PID of sleep and list its File Descriptor Table; stop sleep with Ctrl+C in the second terminal. Check: 0 points to fruits.txt, 1 to /tmp/out.txt and 2 to /dev/null: the shell changed the table before sleep started. → The /proc File System · Redirects A pipe seen from inside: in the second terminal, run sleep 800 | sleep 900; in the first terminal, find the PIDs of the two sleep processes (look in man pgrep for the option that also prints the command line, so you can tell them apart); list the File Descriptor Tables of both processes; stop them with Ctrl+C in the second terminal. Check: 1 of sleep 800 and 0 of sleep 900 point to the same pipe:[...], with the same number. → The /proc File System · Pipes What does less read: in the second terminal, open /etc/services (the list of the network services and their ports) with less; in the first terminal, find the PID of less; list the files that less has open, and print its command line and its current directory, using /proc; quit less with q. Check: besides 0, 1 and 2, less has /etc/services open, at file descriptor 3 or higher. → The /proc File System Where is the other shell: in the second terminal, go to ~/lab03/Music and print the PID of the shell; in the first terminal, find the current directory of that shell, using /proc; open its environ file with less and find the value of the HOME variable: less warns that it may be a binary file, because of the \0 bytes between the variables, so answer y; the \0 bytes show up as ^@, and you search with /. Check: cwd points to /home/student/lab03/Music, and environ has HOME=/home/student. → The /proc File System Save top: run top so that it prints its list only once and does not update it (see the tip in top); keep only the first 15 lines of its output, and save them into Reports/top.txt, in the same command line. Check: Reports/top.txt has 15 lines, starting with the summary of top. → top · Pipes htop in depth: In htop: hide the threads; show only your processes; sort them by memory; choose the bash of the first terminal (the PID printed by echo $$) and show its open files (if htop says that it cannot run lsof, install it with sudo dnf install lsof); add the PPID column: press F2, go to Screens, choose PPID in Available Columns, press Enter to add it, then leave the menu with F10. Check: the open files of bash are the same as in ls -l /proc/$$/fd, and the PPID of bash is the PID of the terminal. → htop Whose processes: count the processes of root with ps, wc -l and a pipe (look in man ps for the option that selects the processes of a user, and use --no-headers, so that wc -l does not also count the line with the names of the columns); count your own processes in the same way; count them again, without --no-headers. Check: root has many more processes than student: most of the system runs as root. Without --no-headers, each number is larger by one. → Listing Processes · Pipes Who runs the processes: list all the processes of the system with ps, printing only the column of the user, without the header line; in the same command line, using sort and uniq, print every user only once, with the number of its processes in front of it, the user with the most processes first. Check: the first line is root, with the same number as ps -u root --no-headers | wc -l, and student is among the first lines; the numbers added up are the same as ps -e --no-headers | wc -l. Some users may show up as numbers instead of names: ps prints the UID when the name is too long for the column. → Listing Processes · Repeated Lines Big files: create Archives/zeros.bin with the first 10 MB of /dev/zero, using head (look in man head for the option that prints a number of bytes instead of lines); create Archives/random.bin with the first 10 MB of /dev/urandom, in the same way; compress both files with xz, keeping the originals; compare the sizes of the four files with ls -lh; delete the four files: they are big. Check: zeros.bin.xz is a few KB, random.bin.xz is still about 10 MB: random data cannot be compressed. → Special Files · Compressing One File Compress into another file: Compress /etc/services (the list of the network services) without copying it and without changing /etc: use the option -c, which writes the compressed data to the standard output, and a redirect. compress it with gzip into Archives/services.gz; compress it with bzip2 into Archives/services.bz2; compress it with xz into Archives/services.xz; put time in front of each of the three commands, and compare the times and the sizes of the files. Check: the three files exist, /etc/services is unchanged, xz makes the smallest file and takes the longest. → Compressing One File Read without extracting: Look in man gzip and man xz for the commands that print the content of a compressed file, without creating any new file. compress /etc/services with gzip -c into Archives/services.gz, and with xz -c into Archives/services.xz; print the content of Archives/services.gz one screen at a time, with less; count the lines of Archives/services.xz; print the first 20 lines of the compressed manual page /usr/share/man/man1/ls.1.gz. Check: the count is the same as wc -l < /etc/services; the manual page is a text file with formatting commands, lines that start with ., like .TH and .SH. → Compressing One File Compression from the name: create Archives/photos.tar.bz2 with Photos, without telling tar the compressor: let it choose the compressor from the extension of the archive (look in man tar for this option); find out the type of the archive with file. Check: file Archives/photos.tar.bz2 says bzip2 compressed data. → Compressed Archives Without the full path: create /tmp/doc.tar.gz with the directory /usr/share/doc/bash (the documentation of bash), so that the names in the archive start with bash/ and not with usr/share/doc/ (look in man tar for the option that changes the directory before adding the files); list the content of the archive. Check: tar tf /tmp/doc.tar.gz lists names that start with bash/. → Archives

Count with /proc: count the directories in /proc whose name is a number (a wildcard can have a range of characters: [0-9] matches one digit; see man 7 glob); count the processes of the system with ps -e --no-headers and wc -l; compare the two numbers. Check: the two numbers are almost the same: every process is a directory in /proc. → The /proc File System The shells of the users: Every line of /etc/passwd has 7 fields separated by :, and the last one is the shell of the user. print only the shell of every user (look in man cut for the options that choose the separator and keep only one field of every line); in the same command line, print every shell only once, with the number of users that have it, the most used first; print only the shells that are used by more than one user. Check: a nologin shell is the first line, with most of the users. You may see both /sbin/nologin and /usr/sbin/nologin: they are the same program (/sbin is a link to usr/sbin), but uniq compares only the text, so it counts them on separate lines. /bin/bash is used by root and student, and the numbers added up are the same as wc -l < /etc/passwd. → Repeated Lines · Pipes Who has the file open: in the second terminal, open /etc/hosts (the names of the computers that the system knows without asking the network) with less; in the first terminal, find the file descriptor that points to /etc/hosts, without using pgrep or ps: search /proc/*/fd with find (look in man find for the test that checks where a symbolic link points to), and throw away the Permission denied errors for the processes of other users; check with ps -p that the number in the path that find prints is the PID of less; quit less with q. Check: find prints a path like /proc/3402/fd/4, and ps -p 3402 shows less. → The /proc File System Back up the configuration: create /tmp/etc.tar.gz with the whole /etc directory (the configuration of the system), except /etc/pki, the directory with the certificates that the system uses to check secure connections, like the https:// websites (look in man tar for the option that leaves files out of the archive); in the same command, save the errors of tar into Reports/etc-errors.txt; count the entries in the archive, with tar tf and wc -l; count only the Permission denied lines in Reports/etc-errors.txt, with grep -c. Check: tar tf /tmp/etc.tar.gz lists etc/passwd and etc/os-release, but nothing from etc/pki. Reports/etc-errors.txt has a Permission denied for every file that only root can read, like /etc/shadow, and two more lines that are not about a file. The first one, tar: Removing leading `/' from member names, only tells you that tar saves /etc/passwd as etc/passwd, so that the archive can be extracted anywhere. The last one, tar: Exiting with failure status due to previous errors, only says that there were errors. This is why you count only the Permission denied lines. → Compressed Archives Strip a directory: create Archives/all.tar.gz with Music, Photos and numbers.txt; create the directory /tmp/flat; extract Archives/all.tar.gz into /tmp/flat so that the files of Music and Photos end up directly in /tmp/flat, without their directories (look in man tar for the option that removes directories from the beginning of the names). Check: tree /tmp/flat shows the five empty files directly under /tmp/flat, but not numbers.txt. --strip-components=1 removes the first part of every name: Music/jazz.mp3 becomes jazz.mp3, but numbers.txt is in the top directory of the archive, so nothing is left of its name, and tar does not extract it (the same happens to the names Music/ and Photos/). → Archives Archives through a pipe: create /tmp/music.tar.gz with the directory Music, in a single command line, so that tar writes the archive, not compressed, to its standard output (an archive file named - means the standard output), gzip compresses it in a pipe, and a redirect saves it; create the directory /tmp/piped; extract /tmp/music.tar.gz into /tmp/piped in another pipe: gunzip -c decompresses it to its standard output, and tar reads the archive from its standard input (an archive file named - means the standard input). Check: file /tmp/music.tar.gz says gzip compressed data, and tree /tmp/piped shows Music. → Pipes · Compressed Archives Clean up: With a single rm command, delete everything that the exercises create in /tmp, without any error for the ones you did not create (look in man rm): danger rm -rf does not ask anything, and what it deletes cannot be recovered. Read the command twice before you press Enter: a space in the wrong place, like rm -rf /tmp /extract instead of rm -rf /tmp/extract, deletes much more than you want. the directories /tmp/extract, /tmp/single, /tmp/gz, /tmp/bz2, /tmp/xz, /tmp/unzipped, /tmp/fruit, /tmp/flat and /tmp/piped; the files /tmp/out.txt, /tmp/doc.tar.gz, /tmp/etc.tar.gz and /tmp/music.tar.gz. Check: rm prints nothing, and ls /tmp no longer shows them. → Managing Files

Why does wc -l < file not print the name of the file? What is the difference between an archive and a compressed file? Why does a .tar.gz have two extensions? In the third lab you learned to redirect what a command reads and writes, and to inspect the processes of the system. In this lab you will look closer at the shell and at the terminal it runs in. You will run commands in the background, stop them and bring them back, and send them signals. You will set variables and see which of them reach the commands you start. At the end you will find out exactly what the shell does with a line of text before a command starts: how it splits it into words, what the quotes and the globs do, and how it finds the program to run. The most important idea of this lab is that the command never sees what you type. The shell reads the line, replaces the variables and the globs, removes the quotes, sets up the redirects, finds the program and only then starts it, with a list of words as its parameters.

Understand what a terminal, a pseudo terminal and a shell are, and use the virtual terminals Send signals to processes with kill command and with the keyboard, and handle a signal with trap Run commands in the background and manage them as jobs with &, jobs, fg, bg and kill %N See how the processes of a terminal are grouped in process groups and sessions, and keep a command running after the terminal closes with nohup Use shell variables and environment variables, with export, unset, printenv and env, and the special parameters $?, $$ and $! Split a command line into its parts: the assignments, the command, its parameters and the redirects Use quotes and \ to control how the shell splits words and replaces variables Select files with globs: *, ?, [...], [!...], ** and {...} Tell built-in commands from external ones with type, and understand how the shell searches the PATH

In the past, a computer was shared by many users. Each of them had a terminal: a keyboard and a screen (or a printer), without a processor, connected to the computer by a cable. These terminals were TeleTypes, and Linux still calls a terminal a TTY. The terminals only sent the keys to the computer and printed what it sent back: all the programs ran on the mainframe. Today, the kernel gives every program that runs in a terminal a terminal device, a special file in /dev. The program reads the keys from it and writes the text to it, through the file descriptors 0, 1 and 2. Device What it is In ps /dev/tty1, /dev/tty2, ... the virtual terminals of the kernel: each one uses the screen and the keyboard of the computer, one at a time tty1 /dev/pts/0, /dev/pts/1, ... the pseudo terminals: one for every terminal window or tab, and for every SSH connection pts/0 /dev/tty not a terminal of its own: a shortcut to the terminal of the process that opens it never: ps shows the real one

A computer today has one screen and one keyboard, but the kernel makes them look like several terminals: the virtual terminals. Each one works like one of the old terminals, with its own login and its own programs, but only one of them is on the screen at a time. The kernel shows only one of them at a time. On /dev/tty1 in the image above, agetty printed the login prompt, and after the login the shell of alice, bash, uses the same terminal. The graphical interface runs in one of the virtual terminals too, usually the first or the second one. Before you leave it, find out which one, so you know how to come back. Run this in a terminal in Sway: [student@fedora ~]$ loginctl show-session $XDG_SESSION_ID -p VTNr VTNr=2 loginctl asks systemd about your login session: here, Sway runs in the second virtual terminal, /dev/tty2. Ctrl+Alt+F<n> switches to the virtual terminal n: Keys Goes to Ctrl+Alt+F3 ... F6 a text mode terminal, /dev/tty3 ... /dev/tty6 Ctrl+Alt+F2 back to Sway, if VTNr is 2 (F1 if it is 1) In a text mode terminal, a program called agetty waits for a user. Log in with your user and password: login checks them and starts your shell, bash. fedora login: student Password: [student@fedora ~]$ tty /dev/tty3 [student@fedora ~]$ exit tty prints the name of the terminal of the shell: this time a virtual terminal, /dev/tty3. exit closes the shell and agetty waits for a new login. Ctrl+Alt+F2 goes back to Sway, with all your windows exactly as you left them: Sway kept running while you were away. caution In a VirtualBox virtual machine, Ctrl+Alt+F3 is caught by your own operating system, not by the virtual machine. Use Host+F3 instead (the Host key is usually the right Ctrl), and Host+F2 to go back. Other virtual machines have a menu to send these keys. tip If you do not know where Sway is, try Ctrl+Alt+F1 and F2. One of them is Sway; the other one shows a login screen or a text terminal.

The graphical interface, Xorg or Wayland (Sway is a Wayland compositor), takes over one of the virtual terminals and draws on the screen through the framebuffer of the kernel. In it, a terminal is a graphical application, a terminal emulator: foot, kitty, ptyxis, alacritty, ghostty, ... Each window of a terminal emulator asks the kernel for a pseudo terminal: it opens /dev/ptmx, and the kernel creates a new /dev/pts/<n>. A pseudo terminal has two ends. The terminal emulator keeps one end, the master, and reads and writes it like a file. The other end, the slave, is the file /dev/pts/<n>: it behaves exactly like a real terminal. When the emulator starts the shell, it redirects /dev/pts/<n> as the 0, 1 and 2 of the shell. The keys you press are written by the emulator into the master, and the shell reads them from the slave. What the shell writes into the slave comes out of the master, and the emulator draws it in its window. The shell does not know that there is a window: it only sees a terminal. [student@fedora ~]$ tty /dev/pts/0 [student@fedora ~]$ ps PID TTY TIME CMD 2817 pts/0 00:00:00 bash 3104 pts/0 00:00:00 ps [student@fedora ~]$ ls /dev/pts 0 1 ptmx [student@fedora ~]$ ls -l /proc/$$/fd/0 lrwx------. 1 student student 64 Oct 20 10:02 /proc/2817/fd/0 -> /dev/pts/0 This shell runs in the first terminal window, /dev/pts/0, and ps shows only the processes of this terminal. There are two windows open, so there are two pseudo terminals, 0 and 1. The standard input of the shell is the pseudo terminal, as you saw in lab 03. tip A pseudo terminal is a file: what you write into it appears in the window of that terminal. With two terminals, echo hello > /dev/pts/1 run in the first one writes hello in the second one.

A signal is a short message that the operating system sends to a process: a number, with a name that starts with SIG. When a signal arrives, the process stops what it is doing and runs the default action of the signal, or, if it has one, its own signal handler, and then continues. Default action What happens to the process Term it ends Core it ends and leaves a copy of its memory (a core dump), for debugging Stop it is paused, until it receives SIGCONT Cont it continues, if it was stopped; otherwise nothing happens Ign nothing, the signal is thrown away info On Fedora, the core dumps do not appear as files in the current directory: systemd-coredump keeps them. coredumpctl list shows them, the newest last. info On Fedora, the core dumps do not appear as files in the current directory: systemd-coredump keeps them. coredumpctl list shows them, the newest last. The signals you will use most often: Number Signal Default action Sent when Can be handled? 1 SIGHUP Term the terminal closed (hang up) yes 2 SIGINT Term you pressed Ctrl+C (interrupt) yes 3 SIGQUIT Core you pressed Ctrl+\ yes 9 SIGKILL Term someone wants the process to end now no 15 SIGTERM Term someone asks the process to end; the default of kill yes 18 SIGCONT Cont fg or bg continues a stopped job yes, but it continues anyway 19 SIGSTOP Stop someone wants the process to stop now no 20 SIGTSTP Stop you pressed Ctrl+Z yes 21 SIGTTIN Stop a background process tried to read from the terminal yes The numbers 18 to 21 are for x86 and ARM computers; other processors use other numbers. Use the names in commands, kill -CONT, not kill -18: they work everywhere. man 7 signal has the full list.

Despite its name, kill sends a signal. Only SIGTERM, its default, asks the process to end. Command What it does kill -l Lists all the signals, with their numbers kill -l <NUMBER> Prints the name of a signal: kill -l 15 prints TERM kill <PID> Sends SIGTERM, the default, to the process kill -KILL <PID> Sends SIGKILL; kill -9 <PID> and kill -SIGKILL <PID> are the same kill -STOP <PID> Stops the process kill -CONT <PID> Continues the stopped process kill <PID1> <PID2> ... Sends the signal (SIGTERM, or the one you give) to several processes kill %<N> Sends the signal to job N of this shell (see jobs) Start sleep 1000 in the second terminal and send it signals from the first one: [student@fedora ~]$ pgrep sleep 3150 [student@fedora ~]$ kill -STOP 3150 [student@fedora ~]$ ps -o pid,stat,cmd -p 3150 PID STAT CMD 3150 T+ sleep 1000 [student@fedora ~]$ kill -CONT 3150 [student@fedora ~]$ ps -o pid,stat,cmd -p 3150 PID STAT CMD 3150 S+ sleep 1000 [student@fedora ~]$ kill 3150 [student@fedora ~]$ ps -o pid,stat,cmd -p 3150 PID STAT CMD SIGSTOP paused sleep: its state became T (stopped). SIGCONT continued it: it is waiting again (S). SIGTERM ended it: ps finds no process with this PID, and the second terminal prints Terminated. caution Use kill -KILL only when kill alone does not work. SIGTERM lets a program clean up before it ends (save its files, delete its temporary files), SIGKILL does not give it any chance.

The terminal turns some keys into signals for the process that runs in the foreground, the one that reads the keyboard: Keys Sends What happens, by default Ctrl+C SIGINT the foreground job ends Ctrl+\ SIGQUIT the foreground job ends, and the system saves a core dump Ctrl+Z SIGTSTP the foreground job is stopped, and the shell shows the prompt (see below) Ctrl+D no signal at the start of a line, end of file: the program reads nothing more [student@fedora ~]$ sleep 100 ^C [student@fedora ~]$ sleep 100 ^\Quit (core dumped) [student@fedora ~]$ sleep 100 ^Z [1]+ Stopped sleep 100 info Ctrl+D at the prompt of the shell is the end of its input: the shell ends, and the terminal window closes.

A program can replace the default action of a signal with its own signal handler: a part of its code that runs when the signal arrives, instead of the default action. A bash script sets a handler with trap, which runs a command or a function.. Create the file ~/lab04/stubborn.sh with nano: #!/bin/bash # the signal handler function no_interruptions_please () { echo "No interruptions please" } # register the signal handler trap no_interruptions_please SIGINT while true; do echo "working" sleep 1 done [student@fedora lab04]$ bash stubborn.sh working working ^CNo interruptions please working ^CNo interruptions please working ^\Quit (core dumped) The script writes working every second, forever. Ctrl+C sends SIGINT: the script runs its handler, prints the message, and keeps working. Ctrl+\ sends SIGQUIT, which has no handler: the script ends. Command What it does trap '<command>' <SIGNAL> Runs command when SIGNAL arrives; the quotes make it one word trap '' <SIGNAL> Ignores the signal trap - <SIGNAL> Goes back to the default action trap -p Prints the handlers info trap keeps the handler as text, and the shell runs that text when the signal arrives, as if you typed it then. The quotes decide when a variable in it is replaced: info SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be handled or ignored: trap cannot change them. This is why kill -KILL always ends a process.

A terminal has one job in the foreground: it reads the keyboard and receives the signals of the keys, and the shell waits for it to end before it shows the prompt again. All the commands you ran so far ran in the foreground. The shell can also start commands in the background. They are called jobs: the shell does not wait for them and shows the prompt right away, so they run at the same time as the commands you type. A job is either running or stopped. A command starts in the foreground (cmd) or in the background (cmd &). Ctrl+Z stops the foreground process and moves it to the background, bg continues a stopped job in the background, and fg brings a job back to the foreground. The rest of this section shows each of them.

Put & at the end of a command to run it in the background: [student@fedora ~]$ sleep 100 & [1] 4242 [student@fedora ~]$ sleep 200 & [2] 4250 [student@fedora ~]$ jobs [1]- Running sleep 100 & [2]+ Running sleep 200 & [student@fedora ~]$ echo $! 4250 [student@fedora ~]$ kill %1 [student@fedora ~]$ [1]- Terminated sleep 100 [1] is the job ID, which exists only in this shell; 4242 is the PID, for the whole system. jobs lists the jobs of this shell: + marks the current job (the last one), - the previous one. $! is the PID of the last job started with &. %1 means job 1: kill %1 sent SIGTERM to it, and the shell said that it ended when it showed the next prompt. Command What it does command & Runs command in the background, as a job jobs Lists the jobs of this shell jobs -l Lists them with their PIDs fg %<N> Brings job N to the foreground (and continues it, if it is stopped) bg %<N> Continues the stopped job N in the background kill %<N> Sends SIGTERM to job N fg, bg Without %<N>, they work on the current job, the one with + caution A job still writes to the same terminal: its output gets mixed with the commands you type. Redirect its output, for example find / -name passwd > found.txt 2> /dev/null &.

A command that runs in the foreground can be moved to the background later: press Ctrl+Z: the command is stopped (SIGTSTP), and the shell prints its job ID, for example [1]+ Stopped, and shows the prompt; find its job ID with jobs; run bg %<N>: the job continues (SIGCONT) in the background. tip fg %<N> brings it back to the foreground. [student@fedora ~]$ sleep 100 > /dev/null ^Z [1]+ Stopped sleep 100 > /dev/null [student@fedora ~]$ jobs [1]+ Stopped sleep 100 > /dev/null [student@fedora ~]$ bg %1 [1]+ sleep 100 > /dev/null & [student@fedora ~]$ jobs [1]+ Running sleep 100 > /dev/null & [student@fedora ~]$ fg %1 sleep 100 > /dev/null ^C After Ctrl+Z, sleep is stopped and the shell shows the prompt. bg continued it in the background (the shell prints it with an & at the end). fg brought it back to the foreground: the shell waits for it again, and Ctrl+C reaches it. tip Ctrl+Z is useful when you forgot the &, or when you want to leave a program for a moment, for example nano or less, run a command, then go back with fg.
documents.s: Stopping and Continuing: fg and bg

documents.t: Only the foreground process can read the keyboard. A job that tries to read it receives SIGTTIN and is stopped: [student@fedora ~]$ cat & [1] 4321 [student@fedora ~]$ [1]+ Stopped cat [student@fedora ~]$ fg cat hello hello ^D cat without parameters reads the keyboard, so it stopped right away. fg brought it to the foreground, where it can read: it printed back every line, until Ctrl+D. info You cannot close a shell that still has stopped jobs at the first try: exit prints There are stopped jobs., and only a second exit closes it (and ends the jobs).

The kernel groups the processes of a terminal in two levels: Group What it is Its ID: the PID of its leader Its leader process group one job: all the processes of one command line, sleep 100 | cat is one group of two processes PGID: the first process of the command line the group leader session all the process groups of one terminal SID, the PID of the shell the session leader: the shell, s in STAT The terminal is the controlling terminal of the session. Its input, and the signals of the keys (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+Z, ...), go to the foreground process group, so they reach every process of the foreground job. + in the STAT column of ps marks the processes of the foreground group. [student@fedora ~]$ echo $$ 3000 [student@fedora ~]$ sleep 100 | cat & [1] 4243 [student@fedora ~]$ ps -o pid,ppid,pgid,sid,tty,stat,comm PID PPID PGID SID TT STAT COMMAND 3000 2990 3000 3000 pts/0 Ss bash 4242 3000 4242 3000 pts/0 S sleep 4243 3000 4242 3000 pts/0 S cat 4250 3000 4250 3000 pts/0 R+ ps bash is the session leader: its PID is the SID of all the processes of the terminal, and it has an s in STAT. sleep and cat are one job, so one group: 4242, the PID of sleep, the first process of the job. ps runs in the foreground (+), in a group of its own.

When the terminal closes, the kernel sends SIGHUP (hang up) to the session leader, the shell. The shell sends SIGHUP to all its jobs, and they end. A command started with nohup ignores SIGHUP, so it keeps running: [student@fedora ~]$ sleep 1000 & [1] 4300 [student@fedora ~]$ nohup sleep 2000 > /dev/null & [2] 4301 nohup: ignoring input Close this terminal window, and look for the two jobs from another terminal: [student@fedora ~]$ pgrep -a sleep 4301 sleep 2000 [student@fedora ~]$ ps -o pid,ppid,sid,tty,comm -p 4301 PID PPID SID TT COMMAND 4301 1 3000 ? sleep sleep 1000 received SIGHUP and ended. sleep 2000 ignored it and keeps running, without a terminal (?); its parent ended, so its new parent is PID 1. info If you do not redirect its output, nohup writes it into the file nohup.out, because the terminal will not exist anymore: nohup: ignoring input and appending output to 'nohup.out'. caution If the shell is killed with SIGKILL, it cannot send SIGHUP to its jobs anymore: they keep running, without a terminal, even without nohup.
documents.s: Closing the Terminal: SIGHUP and nohup

documents.t: Every process has an environment: a list of variables, each written as NAME=value. Programs read it to configure themselves: HOME tells them the home directory of the user, LANG the language, and PATH where to look for programs. The names are case-sensitive (HOME and home are different variables) and, by convention, in UPPER CASE. A process receives its environment from its parent when it starts: usually a copy of the parent's environment. From then on the two are separate: a change in one does not reach the other. Command What it does printenv Prints all the environment variables printenv <NAME> Prints the value of one variable env Prints all the environment variables, like printenv echo $NAME The shell replaces $NAME with its value, then echo prints it [student@fedora ~]$ printenv HOME /home/student [student@fedora ~]$ echo "I am $USER, my shell is $SHELL" I am student, my shell is /bin/bash [student@fedora ~]$ env | wc -l 35

The shell has two kinds of variables: shell variables: they exist only inside this shell; environment variables: they are part of the environment, so every command started from this shell receives a copy. Syntax What it does NAME=value Creates a shell variable, or changes the value of an existing variable export NAME Makes the variable an environment variable: every command started from now on receives it export NAME=value Both at once NAME=value command An environment variable only for command; the shell does not keep it unset NAME Deletes the variable, from the shell and from the environment $NAME Replaced by the shell with the value, or with nothing if the variable does not exist ${NAME} The same, with clear limits: "${NAME}_old" is the value followed by _old; "$NAME_old" is the variable NAME_old [student@fedora ~]$ GREETING=hello [student@fedora ~]$ echo $GREETING hello [student@fedora ~]$ bash -c 'echo "child: $GREETING"' child: [student@fedora ~]$ export GREETING [student@fedora ~]$ bash -c 'echo "child: $GREETING"' child: hello [student@fedora ~]$ unset GREETING [student@fedora ~]$ echo "[$GREETING]" [] GREETING=hello created a shell variable, and the shell replaced $GREETING with hello. bash -c '...' starts a new shell, a child, that runs the text between the quotes. The child did not receive GREETING: it was not part of the environment. After export, the child received a copy of it. After unset, the variable does not exist anymore, and $GREETING is replaced with nothing. danger No spaces around =. GREETING = hello runs the command GREETING, with the parameters = and hello: bash: GREETING: command not found. Put the value between quotes when it has spaces: GREETING="good morning". info A process can change only its own environment, and the environment of the children it starts after that. A child can never change a variable of its parent: this is why export and unset are commands of the shell, not programs.

NAME=value written before a command puts the variable only in the environment of that command: [student@fedora ~]$ date +%H:%M 11:47 [student@fedora ~]$ TZ=Asia/Tokyo date +%H:%M 18:47 [student@fedora ~]$ echo "[$TZ]" [] [student@fedora ~]$ ls /nope ls: cannot access '/nope': No such file or directory [student@fedora ~]$ LANG=ro_RO.UTF-8 ls /nope ls: nu se poate accesa '/nope': Fișier sau director inexistent TZ (time zone) changed the time zone only for that date; the shell did not keep it. LANG changed the language of the messages of ls (if the Romanian language is installed).

When the prompt shows up, the shell already has many variables, set when you logged in or by its startup files: Variable Value HOME your home directory, ~ USER your user name SHELL your shell, from /etc/passwd PWD, OLDPWD the current directory and the previous one (cd - goes to OLDPWD) PATH the directories with the programs, separated by : (see The PATH Search) LANG the language and the encoding of the characters PS1 the prompt; a shell variable, not exported tip PS1 is the text of the prompt, with some special sequences: \u is the user, \h the computer, \w the current directory, \$ is $ (or # for root). Try PS1='\u in \w \$ '. The change lasts until you close the terminal.

The shell sets a few more values that you can only read: Parameter Value $? the exit code of the last command: 0 means success, anything else an error $$ the PID of the shell $! the PID of the job most recently sent to the background, with & or bg [student@fedora ~]$ ls /nope ls: cannot access '/nope': No such file or directory [student@fedora ~]$ echo $? 2 [student@fedora ~]$ echo $? 0 ls failed, with the exit code 2. The second echo $? prints the exit code of the first echo, which succeeded: $? changes after every command.

Before a command starts, the shell reads the whole line and splits it into parts: [student@fedora lab04]$ LANG=C sort -r "$HOME/my notes.txt" my\ list.txt *.csv > sorted.txt 2> errors.txt Part In the example What it is assignments LANG=C NAME=value words at the start: variables only for this command the command sort the first word that is not an assignment or a redirect the parameters -r, "$HOME/my notes.txt", my\ list.txt, *.csv everything else: options, file names, texts redirects > sorted.txt, 2> errors.txt a redirect and the word after it; they are for the shell, not for the command, and can be anywhere Then, step by step: it splits the line into words at the spaces, except inside quotes and after a \; it sets apart the assignments and the redirects; it replaces $NAME and ~ with their values; it splits again the values of the variables that were not between quotes; it expands the globs (*.csv) into the names of the matching files; it removes the quotes and the \; it sets up the redirects and runs the command, with the words that are left as its parameters. sort receives 5 parameters: -r, /home/student/my notes.txt, my list.txt, a.csv and b.csv. It never sees the quotes, the $, the * or the redirects. tip To see the words that a command receives, use printf '[%s]\n' instead of the command: it prints every parameter between brackets, on its own line. [student@fedora lab04]$ printf '[%s]\n' -r "$HOME/my notes.txt" my\ list.txt *.csv [-r] [/home/student/my notes.txt] [my list.txt] [a.csv] [b.csv]

The redirects can be written anywhere in the line, even before the command, and the shell applies them from left to right: [student@fedora lab04]$ 2> errors.txt ls > list.txt /nope . [student@fedora lab04]$ ls /nope > all.txt 2>&1 [student@fedora lab04]$ ls /nope 2>&1 > all.txt ls: cannot access '/nope': No such file or directory The first line is the same as ls /nope . > list.txt 2> errors.txt. > all.txt 2>&1: first 1 goes to all.txt, then 2 goes where 1 goes now, also into all.txt. 2>&1 > all.txt: first 2 goes where 1 goes now, the display, then only 1 changes to all.txt. The error is on the display.

Some characters have a special meaning for the shell: the space, $, *, ?, [, {, ~, >, <, |, &, ;, #, ', " and \. Quotes and \ turn the special meaning off: Written as What it does '...' single quotes: everything inside is plain text, nothing is replaced "..." double quotes: $NAME is still replaced, but the result stays one word; globs are not expanded \ the next character is plain text: \ is a space that does not split, \$ is a $ With NAME="Alice Smith" (three spaces), this is what echo receives: You type echo receives Why echo $NAME Alice, Smith no quotes: replaced, then split at the spaces echo "$NAME" Alice Smith double quotes: replaced, one word, the spaces are kept echo '$NAME' $NAME single quotes: nothing is replaced echo \$NAME $NAME \$: the $ is just a character echo my\ file.txt my file.txt \ : the space does not split echo "\$NAME is $NAME" $NAME is Alice Smith inside "...", \$ is a $, $NAME is replaced echo "it's" 'say "hi"' it's, say "hi" each kind of quotes protects the other one echo 'a\b' a\b inside '...', \ is just a character [student@fedora ~]$ NAME="Alice Smith" [student@fedora ~]$ echo $NAME Alice Smith [student@fedora ~]$ echo "$NAME" Alice Smith [student@fedora ~]$ printf '[%s]\n' $NAME [Alice] [Smith] echo $NAME received two words and printed them with one space between them: the three spaces were lost. tip Put every variable between double quotes, "$NAME", unless you really want it split into words. A file name with a space in a variable breaks a command without them: rm $FILE with FILE="my notes.txt" tries to delete my and notes.txt.

A glob is a pattern for file names. The shell replaces it with the names of the matching files, in alphabetical order, before the command starts. In this directory: [student@fedora glob]$ ls docs notes.txt photo1.png photo2.png photo3.png photoA.png report.md todo.txt Glob Matches echo receives *.txt *: any characters, or none (but not /) notes.txt, todo.txt photo?.png ?: exactly one character photo1.png, photo2.png, photo3.png, photoA.png photo[12].png [12]: one character, 1 or 2 photo1.png, photo2.png photo[0-9].png [0-9]: one character in the range photo1.png, photo2.png, photo3.png photo[!0-9].png [!0-9]: one character not in the range ([^0-9] also works) photoA.png docs/**/*.txt **: any directories, at any depth (needs shopt -s globstar) docs/2026/exam.txt, docs/plan.txt {a,b,c}.pdf {...}: one word for each, even if the file does not exist a.pdf, b.pdf, c.pdf *.pdf no file matches *.pdf, the glob as it is caution When no file matches, bash gives the glob as it is to the command: ls *.pdf prints ls: cannot access '*.pdf': No such file or directory. Other shells, like zsh, print an error and do not run the command at all. info * and ? do not match the . at the beginning of a hidden file: * does not include .bashrc, but .* does. {...} is not a glob: it makes the words even if there are no files, which is useful to create them, for example mkdir -p 2026/{jan,feb,mar} or touch photo{4..6}.png ({4..6} is 4 5 6). ** works only after shopt -s globstar; without it, it is the same as *. Between quotes, a glob is plain text: echo "*.txt" prints *.txt. This is how you give a pattern to a command that understands it by itself, like find . -name "*.txt".

Not every command is a program: Kind What it is Examples Help built-in command part of the shell: it runs inside it, without a new process cd, export, unset, exit, jobs, fg, bg, trap, type help <name> some are built in only to be faster, and also exist as programs echo, printf, kill, pwd external command an executable file on the disk, found in PATH; the shell starts it as a child process ls, sort, grep, sleep, bash man <name> type tells which one a command is: [student@fedora ~]$ type cd cd is a shell builtin [student@fedora ~]$ type sort sort is /usr/bin/sort [student@fedora ~]$ type ls ls is aliased to `ls --color=auto' [student@fedora ~]$ type -a echo echo is a shell builtin echo is /usr/bin/echo cd is built in, sort is the file /usr/bin/sort. ls is an alias: a short name for another command line, here ls --color=auto. -a shows all the meanings of the name: echo is built in, and there is also a program with the same name. The shell uses the first one. info cd, export, unset and exit must be built in: they change the shell itself, its current directory, its variables, or stop it. A program started by the shell is a child process, and a child cannot change its parent.

The kernel can only start a program from its path. When the first word is a name, the shell has to find the file: if the word has a /, it is a path: absolute (/usr/bin/sort) or relative to the current directory (./hello, bin/hello, ../tools/hello), used as it is; otherwise, if it is an alias or a built-in command, the shell runs it itself; otherwise, the shell searches the directories of the PATH variable, from left to right, and runs the first file with that name; if no directory has it: command not found. [student@fedora ~]$ echo $PATH /home/student/.local/bin:/home/student/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin [student@fedora ~]$ cd ~/lab04 [student@fedora lab04]$ ls bin hello [student@fedora lab04]$ hello bash: hello: command not found [student@fedora lab04]$ bin/hello Hello! [student@fedora lab04]$ PATH="$PATH:$HOME/lab04/bin" [student@fedora lab04]$ hello Hello! [student@fedora lab04]$ type hello hello is /home/student/lab04/bin/hello The shell does not look in the current directory, so hello alone was not found. bin/hello has a /, so it is a path, and the shell ran it. After adding ~/lab04/bin at the end of PATH, the shell found hello there. caution Add directories to PATH, never replace it: PATH=~/lab04/bin alone leaves the shell without /usr/bin, and ls, cat and almost every other command become command not found. Close the terminal and open a new one to get the old PATH back. tip On Fedora, ~/.local/bin and ~/bin are already in PATH: copy a program of your own there and it works from any directory, in every new terminal.

Problem Solution Ctrl+C does not stop a program It handles or ignores SIGINT: try Ctrl+\, or Ctrl+Z followed by kill %1; as a last resort, kill -KILL <PID> from another terminal kill does not end a process It handles SIGTERM: use kill -KILL <PID> A stopped process does not react to kill It receives the signal when it continues: kill -CONT <PID>, or use kill -KILL <PID> bash: kill: (4242) - Operation not permitted The process belongs to another user bash: kill: %1: no such job or fg: current: no such job The job belongs to another terminal (every shell has its own jobs), or it has already ended; use the PID [1]+ Stopped right after command & The job tries to read the keyboard: bring it to the foreground with fg, or redirect its input There are stopped jobs. when you close the shell Continue or end them (fg, kill %N); a second exit ends them A job writes over the commands you type Redirect its output to a file, or to /dev/null bash: NAME: command not found after NAME = value No spaces around = A child does not see a variable It is a shell variable: export it bash: <command>: command not found Check the name, then echo $PATH: the directory of the program is not in PATH, or PATH was replaced; open a new terminal A file in the current directory is command not found The shell does not search the current directory: run it as ./name cannot access '*.pdf' No file matches the glob, so the command received it as it is A name with a space becomes two files Put it, or the variable that holds it, between double quotes The shell shows > and waits A quote is not closed: close it, or press Ctrl+C and type the line again

The exercises get harder as you go: 🧪 First Steps (exercises 1 - 23) goes once through everything in this lab, with easy exercises; 🏠 Going Further (exercises 24 - 51) has more exercises to do at home, harder as you go; 📝 Challenges (exercises 52 - 62) has the hardest ones. Exercise 1 creates the files and directories that all the other exercises start from. Run the commands in ~/lab04, unless the exercise says otherwise. If you change or delete one of the files from exercise 1, run its commands again to get it back. Some exercises ask for things that the lab does not show you, for example an option that is not in the tables above. Find it in the manual page of the command (man <command>), as explained in Searching in a Manual Page in lab 02. jobs, fg, bg, trap, export and the other built-in commands do not have a manual page of their own: use help <command>, for example help trap, or search man bash. Keep two terminals side by side in Sway: the first one to run the commands, and the second one to run the commands that you inspect, or to check the results. Many exercises use the PID of a process: it is different on your computer, use the one that pgrep, ps or $! prints for you. danger Do not use sudo to send signals: sudo kill can end the processes of the system. Send signals only to your own processes, and check the PID twice before kill -KILL.

The practice tree: run these commands to create the files used in the exercises (copy them from the browser with Ctrl+C and paste them in the terminal with Ctrl+Shift+V): mkdir -p ~/lab04/bin ~/lab04/glob/docs/2026 cd ~/lab04 printf 'pear
fig
' > 'my notes.txt' printf 'cherry
Banana
apple
' > 'my list.txt' printf 'banana,3
apple,5
' > a.csv printf 'cherry,1
kiwi,7
' > b.csv printf '#!/bin/bash
echo Hello!
' > bin/hello chmod +x bin/hello cat > stubborn.sh << 'EOF' #!/bin/bash # the signal handler function no_interruptions_please () { echo "No interruptions please" } # register the signal handler trap no_interruptions_please SIGINT while true; do echo "working" sleep 1 done EOF cd ~/lab04/glob touch notes.txt todo.txt report.md photo1.png photo2.png photo3.png photoA.png docs/plan.txt docs/2026/exam.txt cd ~/lab04 run tree in ~/lab04; print stubborn.sh with cat. Check: you see bin/hello, the two .csv files, my list.txt, my notes.txt, stubborn.sh and the glob directory with 9 files; stubborn.sh is the script from Handling a Signal. chmod +x makes hello a program that can be run (you will learn about it in the lab about permissions). → Navigation Terminals Which terminal: print the terminal of the shell, in both terminals; list the pseudo terminals in /dev/pts; open a third terminal and list them again, then close it. Check: each shell has its own /dev/pts/<n>; the third terminal adds one more number to the list, and its number disappears after you close it. → Terminal Emulators Write to another terminal: find the terminal of the second shell, with tty; from the first terminal, write hello from the first terminal into the second one, with echo and a redirect. Check: the text appears in the second terminal, without anything typed there. → Terminal Emulators A virtual terminal: in a terminal in Sway, find out in which virtual terminal Sway runs, with loginctl; switch to the third virtual terminal with Ctrl+Alt+F3 (Host+F3 in VirtualBox); log in as student, print the name of the terminal and list its processes with ps; log out with exit; switch back to Sway, using the number that loginctl printed. Check: VTNr is 1 or 2; tty prints /dev/tty3, and ps shows a bash on tty3; after exit, the terminal asks for a login again; back in Sway, your windows are exactly as you left them. → Virtual Terminals Signals The list of signals: list all the signals with kill; print the name of signal 9 and the number of SIGCONT, with kill -l. Check: signal 9 is KILL, and CONT is 18. → Sending a Signal Stop and continue: in the second terminal, run sleep 1000; in the first terminal, find its PID and stop it with a signal; show its state with ps -o pid,stat,cmd -p <PID>, and look at the second terminal; continue it, show its state again, and run jobs in the second terminal; end it with kill %1 in the second terminal. Check: the state is T after SIGSTOP and S after SIGCONT, without the +. As soon as sleep stopped, the second shell printed [1]+ Stopped (signal), took the terminal back and showed the prompt, so after SIGCONT, jobs shows sleep as Running in the background. → Sending a Signal Keys and signals: run sleep 100 and end it with Ctrl+C; run it again and end it with Ctrl+\; run it again and stop it with Ctrl+Z; list the jobs. Check: the terminal shows ^C after Ctrl+C, Quit (core dumped) after Ctrl+\ (only Quit if core dumps are turned off), and Stopped after Ctrl+Z; sleep is still in the list of jobs. End it with kill %1. → Keys That Send Signals A stubborn script: run bash stubborn.sh; press Ctrl+C a few times; stop it with Ctrl+\. Check: Ctrl+C prints No interruptions please and the script keeps working; Ctrl+\ ends it. → Handling a Signal Foreground and background Two jobs: start sleep 300 and sleep 400 in the background; list the jobs, and then the jobs with their PIDs; print the PID of the last job with $!; end the first job using its job ID; end the second job too, and list the jobs again. Check: jobs shows [1] and [2], with + at [2]; $! is the PID of sleep 400; after the next command, the shell prints [1]- Terminated; at the end, jobs prints nothing. → Starting a Job To the background and back: run sleep 200 > /dev/null in the foreground; stop it with the keyboard; continue it in the background, and check with jobs that it runs; bring it back to the foreground, and end it with the keyboard. Check: jobs shows Stopped, then Running; after fg, the prompt does not show up until you press Ctrl+C. → Stopping and Continuing The current job: start sleep 300, sleep 400 and sleep 500 in the background; list the jobs, and find the current one; run fg without a job ID, and end the job with Ctrl+C; list the jobs again, and end the others with kill. Check: the current job (+) is sleep 500, the last one started, and fg brought it to the foreground; after it ended, sleep 400 became the current job. → Starting a Job Sessions Session and groups: print the PID of your shell; start sleep 100 | cat in the background; list the processes of the terminal with the columns pid, ppid, pgid, sid, tty, stat and comm. Check: all the processes have the PID of the shell as their SID; sleep and cat have the same PGID, the PID of sleep; bash has s and ps has + in STAT. → Sessions and Process Groups Close the terminal: open a new terminal and start sleep 1000 & and nohup sleep 2000 > /dev/null & in it; close the window of this terminal; in another terminal, look for the two sleep processes; end sleep 2000 with kill. Check: only sleep 2000 is still running, without a terminal (?). Its parent ended, so it was adopted: its new parent is PID 1, or a process that adopts orphans, like systemd --user (see which one with ps -o pid,comm -p <PPID>). → Closing the Terminal Variables Read variables: print HOME, USER and SHELL with printenv; print the sentence I am student and I live in /home/student with echo and the variables USER and HOME; count the environment variables. Check: the sentence has your user and your home directory; there are a few dozen variables. → Environment Variables Shell variable or environment variable: set the shell variable COLOR to blue, and print it; check with printenv COLOR and with bash -c 'echo "$COLOR"' whether it is in the environment; export it, and check again; delete it, and print it again. Check: before export, printenv prints nothing and the child prints an empty line; after it, both print blue; after unset, echo prints an empty line. → Shell Variables and export Only for one command: print the time with date +%H:%M; print the time in Tokyo and in New York (America/New_York), by setting TZ only for date; print TZ. Check: the three times are different, and TZ is empty in the shell. → A Variable for One Command Exit codes: run ls ~/lab04 and print its exit code; run ls /nope and print its exit code; run grep apple a.csv and grep pear a.csv, and print the exit code after each of them; run echo $? twice in a row. Check: ls has the exit code 0, then 2; grep has 0 when it finds the text and 1 when it does not; the second echo $? always prints 0. → Special Parameters The command line The words of a command: Use printf '[%s]
' to see the words that the shell gives to a command: printf '[%s]
' one two three; printf '[%s]
' "one two three"; printf '[%s]
' ~ "~" '$HOME' "$HOME". Check: the first line gives 3 words, the second one only 1, with the spaces kept; ~ and "$HOME" become /home/student, "~" and '$HOME' stay as they are. → The Command Line · Quoting and Escaping Quotes and variables: set NAME="Alice Smith"; print it with echo, without quotes, between double quotes and between single quotes; print the text $NAME is Alice Smith with a single echo and one pair of double quotes. Check: without quotes, the three spaces become one; between double quotes they are kept; between single quotes echo prints $NAME; the last echo prints $NAME is Alice Smith, with the three spaces. → Quoting and Escaping A dollar sign: Print the text The price is $5 with echo: first with double quotes and nothing else, and see what goes wrong; with single quotes; with a \ and no quotes; with double quotes and a \. Check: step 1 prints The price is: the shell replaced $5 with nothing. $5 is the fifth positional parameter, a parameter given to a script, and it is empty in your shell. Single quotes and \ turn off the meaning of $, so steps 2, 3 and 4 print The price is $5. → Quoting and Escaping Globs: Go to ~/lab04/glob and, with echo, print: all the .png files; the photos with a single digit after photo; the photos whose name does not have a digit after photo; all the files whose name has exactly 8 characters (count the extension too); all the .pdf files; the names photo7.png and photo8.png, with {...}. Check: photoA.png is in the first and the third list, not in the second one; the fourth list is todo.txt; the fifth echo prints *.pdf, because no file matches; the last one prints both names, even if the files do not exist. → Globbing Built-in or external: find out with type what cd, ls, sort, type and sleep are; show all the meanings of kill and of echo; print the PATH, and find in which of its directories sort is. Check: cd and type are built in, ls is an alias, sort and sleep are in /usr/bin; kill and echo are built in, and also exist as programs in /usr/bin. For a program you already ran, type says hashed, for example sleep is hashed (/usr/bin/sleep): the shell remembers where it found it. → Built-in and External Commands · The PATH Search Command not found: run sl (a typo of ls), and print the exit code; find out with type whether sl exists; run /usr/bin/nope, and print the exit code. Check: the shell searched all the directories of PATH and found no sl: the exit code is 127, the code of the shell for command not found; /usr/bin/nope is a path that does not exist, and its exit code is 127 too. If the shell offers to install a package for sl, answer N. → The PATH Search · Special Parameters

The terminal in ps: list the processes of the terminal with ps; print the 0, 1 and 2 file descriptors of the shell, from /proc/$$/fd. In the fourth lab you learned what the shell does with a command line, and how it starts the programs and sends them signals. In this lab you will find out with which user id these programs are running. You will look at the users and the groups of the system, at the files that keep them, /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow and /etc/group, and at how the system checks a password without ever storing it. You will run commands as root with sudo, create new users, and then decide who may read, write and run your files, with chmod, chown and umask. At the end you will meet the special permissions: the setuid bit that lets passwd change your password, the setgid bit for shared directories and the sticky bit of /tmp. The most important idea of this lab is that the kernel does not know any names. Every process carries a label, the number of its user (the UID) and the numbers of its groups, and every file has an owner, a group and three sets of permissions. Every time a process opens a file, the kernel compares the two. The most important idea of this lab is that the kernel does not know any names, only numbers. Every process carries a label: the number of its user (the UID) and the numbers of its groups (the GIDs). Every file keeps the number of its owner, the number of its group, and three sets of permissions: for the owner, for the group and for everybody else. Every time a process opens a file, the kernel compares the label of the process with the owner and the group of the file, picks one of the three sets, and checks if it allows what the process asks for.

The lab computers run Fedora, with the Sway window manager, and all the examples in this lab come from them. At home, you may use Fedora or Ubuntu: every command in this lab works on both, but some names, defaults and outputs are different. When an example or a check does not match what you see on Ubuntu, look for it in this table first: Fedora Ubuntu the prompt [student@fedora ~]$ student@ubuntu:~$, in color the group of the administrators, who may sudo wheel, GID 10 sudo, GID 27 (you are also in adm, cdrom, ...) the . after the permissions in ls -l, context= in id shown: the SELinux labels not shown the shell of a new user made with useradd /bin/bash /bin/sh, unless you give -s /bin/bash a new home directory drwx------ (700) drwxr-x--- (750) /etc/shadow ---------- root root -rw-r----- root shadow /usr/bin/sudo ---s--x--x (4111) -rwsr-xr-x (4755) a password not set yet, or locked with passwd -l !! in front of the hash, or alone ! in front of the hash, or alone the umask of a regular user 0022 0002 installing a package sudo dnf install <PACKAGE> sudo apt install <PACKAGE> Your user may also have another name than student: use your own name wherever the lab says student.

For you, a user is a name, like student. For the kernel, a user is only a number, the UID (User ID). Every process carries the UID of the user that started it, as a label, for its whole lifetime, and a child process inherits the label of its parent. When a process asks the kernel to do something, to open a file or to send a signal, the kernel looks at this label and decides if the process is allowed to do it. Users are not only people. Many services of the system run as a user of their own: if one of them has a bug, or is attacked, it can only touch its own files, not the files of the other services or of the people.

Command What it prints whoami the user name associated with the current effective user ID id the whole label of the process: the UID, the primary group (GID) and all the groups, with their names id -u, id -g only the UID, only the GID of the primary group id -un only the name of the user, like whoami id -nG only the names of the groups id <USER>, groups <USER> the label of a user, read from the users and groups databases groups the names of your groups, like id -nG [student@fedora ~]$ whoami student [student@fedora ~]$ id uid=1000(student) gid=1000(student) groups=1000(student),10(wheel) context=unconfined_u:unconfined_r:unconfined_t:s0-s0:c0.c1023 [student@fedora ~]$ id root uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root) student has the UID 1000 and the primary group student, with the GID 1000. It is also a member of the group wheel: on Fedora, the members of wheel are the administrators, who may use sudo (see sudo). context=... is the SELinux label of the process, a second security system that Fedora uses. This lab does not need it, and Ubuntu does not show it. root is the user with the UID 0, the administrator.
