documents.t: UID Kind Used for Examples on Fedora 0 root the administrator, the kernel skips most of the checks for it root 1 - 999 system users services; they cannot log in, because their shell is nologin bin, daemon, dbus, chrony 1000 - ... regular users people student 65534 nobody files whose real owner is unknown, and processes that must have no rights nobody These ranges are only a convention: for the kernel, every UID except 0 is the same. They are set in /etc/login.defs, the settings file of useradd and of the other commands that create users, which take the next free UID from the right range: [student@fedora ~]$ grep -E '^(UID|SYS_UID)_(MIN|MAX)' /etc/login.defs UID_MIN 1000 UID_MAX 60000 SYS_UID_MIN 201 SYS_UID_MAX 999

ps shows the user of every process in the column USER (or UID, as a number): [student@fedora ~]$ ps -o user,uid,pid,ppid,comm USER UID PID PPID COMMAND student 1000 2817 2805 bash student 1000 3104 2817 ps [student@fedora ~]$ ps -eo user | sort | uniq -c 4 chrony 2 dbus ... 156 root 51 student bash and ps run as student: ps is a child of bash, and it inherited its label. ps -eo user prints the user of every process; sort | uniq -c counts them (see Pipes in lab 03). Most of the processes of the system run as root. info ps gets only the UIDs from the kernel. To print a name, it looks up each UID in the users database; if the UID is not there, for example because the user was deleted, it prints the number. ls -l, id and the prompt do the same.

The label of a process is more than one UID and a list of groups. For every process, the kernel keeps a small record, the credentials of the process: four UIDs, four GIDs and the list of the supplementary groups. Think of it as an ID card that the kernel keeps for the process: the kernel looks at it every time the process asks for something, and the process cannot change it as it likes. Credential What it is real UID and GID the user who started the process, and their primary group; programs read them to find out who you are effective UID and GID the ones that the kernel checks, when the process opens a file or sends a signal saved UID and GID a spare copy of the effective ones, made when the program starts, so that it can put its rights aside for a while and take them back file system UID and GID used only for files; on Linux, they always follow the effective ones, so you can ignore them supplementary groups the other groups of the process, checked together with the effective GID; copied from the groups database at login, and by su and sudo note For your shell, the four UIDs are all 1000 and the four GIDs are all 1000. Why does the kernel keep four copies of the same number? Because they are not always the same: a program with the setuid bit, like passwd, changes the effective and the saved UID, but keeps the real one. login, su and sudo do something else: they change all of them, for the shell or the command that they start. Which Credentials Are Checked​ The kernel does not look at all the credentials every time. It depends on what the process asks for: opening a file: the effective UID is compared with the owner of the file, and the effective GID and the supplementary groups with the group of the file (see Which Permissions Apply?); sending a signal, with kill: the real or the effective UID of the sender must be the real or the saved UID of the target. You can end a passwd that you started, even if it runs as root, because its real UID is yours; bob cannot; changing its own UIDs: a process that is not root may only take a UID that it already has, its real, its effective or its saved one. A process cannot make itself root. Only a process whose effective UID is 0 may take any UID. How the Credentials Change​ A process gets its credentials from its parent. This table shows what happens to them at each step of the life of a process, and the only two cases that change them: When What happens to the UIDs fork, a new child the child gets a copy of the credentials of its parent exec of a regular program nothing changes exec of a program with the setuid bit the effective and the saved UID become the owner of the executable file; the real UID is inherited from the parent process; the setgid bit does the same for the GIDs, with the group of the file (see setuid) a process whose effective UID is 0 calls setgid(), initgroups() and setuid() all the GIDs, the supplementary groups and all the UIDs change, in this order: this is how login, su and sudo give a process the label of a user (see Logging In and sudo) Seeing the Credentials​ There are two ways to see the credentials of a process: [student@fedora ~]$ ps -o pid,ruser,euser,suser,comm -p $$ PID RUSER EUSER SUSER COMMAND 2817 student student student bash [student@fedora ~]$ grep -E '^(Uid|Gid|Groups):' /proc/$$/status Uid: 1000 1000 1000 1000 Gid: 1000 1000 1000 1000 Groups: 10 1000 ps -o takes the names of the columns: ruser is the real user, euser the effective one and suser the saved one. man ps lists all of them, for the UIDs, the GIDs and the groups, in the section STANDARD FORMAT SPECIFIERS. The Uid: and Gid: lines of /proc/<PID>/status have 4 numbers: real, effective, saved and file system; Groups: has the supplementary groups (man 5 proc). Everybody can read the status file of any process. Try to make a process root without any help. python3 can ask the kernel for its UIDs, with os.getresuid() (get real, effective and saved UID), and to change them, with os.setuid(): [student@fedora ~]$ python3 -c 'import os; print(os.getresuid()); os.setuid(0)' (1000, 1000, 1000) Traceback (most recent call last): File "<string>", line 1, in <module> import os; print(os.getresuid()); os.setuid(0) ~~~~~~~~~^^^ PermissionError: [Errno 1] Operation not permitted The kernel refuses: 0 is none of the three UIDs of the process. The only ways to get root are to start a program that already runs as root, like sudo, or one with the setuid bit, like passwd.

The local users are kept in /etc/passwd, a text file with one user on every line, and the fields separated by :. Everyone can read it, because every program that shows a user name needs it. [student@fedora ~]$ ls -l /etc/passwd -rw-r--r--. 1 root root 2245 Oct 20 09:12 /etc/passwd [student@fedora ~]$ head -3 /etc/passwd root:x:0:0:Super User:/root:/bin/bash bin:x:1:1:bin:/bin:/usr/sbin/nologin daemon:x:2:2:daemon:/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin [student@fedora ~]$ grep student /etc/passwd student:x:1000:1000:Student:/home/student:/bin/bash Field In the example What it is 1 student the user name, the one you log in with 2 x the password: x means that it is kept in /etc/shadow 3 1000 the UID 4 1000 the GID of the primary group 5 Student the GECOS field: the full name, sometimes followed by the room and phone numbers, with , 6 /home/student the home directory: the current directory after login, ~ and $HOME 7 /bin/bash the shell, the program started after login; /usr/sbin/nologin refuses the login info The . after the permissions, -rw-r--r--., means that the file has an SELinux label. You will see it on almost every file on Fedora: ignore it in this lab. Ubuntu does not show it.

/etc/passwd is not the only place where users can be kept: in a university or a company, the accounts are usually on a server in the network (LDAP, Active Directory, ...). That is why no program do not read /etc/passwd directly by themselves: they ask the C library, with getpwnam() (from a name to a user) and getpwuid() (from a UID to a user). The C library reads /etc/nsswitch.conf to find out where to look for the users, the passwords and the groups, and in which order. So ls, ps and id work the same way whether a user is kept in /etc/passwd or on a server. [student@fedora ~]$ grep -E '^(passwd|shadow|group):' /etc/nsswitch.conf passwd: files systemd shadow: files group: files systemd files means the files in /etc, systemd the users that systemd creates by itself (your system may also have sss, a network server). getent (get entries) asks the C library, exactly like ls and id do, so it finds a user wherever it is kept: Command Finds getent passwd <NAME> or <UID> the user with this name, or this UID getent passwd all the users getent group <NAME> or <GID> the group with this name, or this GID getent group all the groups sudo getent shadow <NAME> the line of the user from /etc/shadow, only for root tip When nothing is found, getent prints nothing, without an error. [student@fedora ~]$ getent passwd 0 root:x:0:0:Super User:/root:/bin/bash [student@fedora ~]$ getent passwd student student:x:1000:1000:Student:/home/student:/bin/bash [student@fedora ~]$ getent passwd nobody nobody:x:65534:65534:Kernel Overflow User:/:/usr/sbin/nologin tip The output has the same format as /etc/passwd. Use getent instead of grep on /etc/passwd when you look for a user: grep root /etc/passwd also finds every line that has root somewhere else, for example in the home directory.

/etc/passwd must be readable by everyone, so the passwords cannot stay there. They are kept in /etc/shadow, that only root can read: [student@fedora ~]$ ls -l /etc/shadow ----------. 1 root root 1207 Oct 20 09:12 /etc/shadow [student@fedora ~]$ cat /etc/shadow cat: /etc/shadow: Permission denied [student@fedora ~]$ sudo grep student /etc/shadow student:$y$j9T$Xr3aB7tPq2LkV9sD1fGh0J$9mQeT4bW1sZxH8cDr5Ny2kLpA7uVq3oEw6iFj0gHt1M:20737:0:99999:7::: On Fedora, /etc/shadow has no permissions at all, ----------: only root can read it, because the kernel skips the checks for root. On Ubuntu, it is -rw-r----- root shadow: the group shadow may read it too, so that a few programs can check passwords without being root. Each line has 9 fields, separated by :: Field In the example What it is 1 student the user name, the same as in /etc/passwd 2 $y$j9T$Xr3a... the hash of the password; !, !! or * at the start means that the account is locked: no password works 3 20737 the day of the last password change, counted from 1 January 1970 4 0 the minimum number of days between two password changes 5 99999 the maximum number of days before the password must be changed, 99999 is never 6 7 how many days before the expiry the user is warned 7 empty how many days after the expiry the account can still be used 8 empty the day when the account expires; empty is never 9 empty reserved chage -l (change age) prints the fields 3 - 8 as dates: [student@fedora ~]$ sudo chage -l student Last password change : Oct 11, 2026 Password expires : never Password inactive : never Account expires : never Minimum number of days between password change : 0 Maximum number of days between password change : 99999 Number of days of warning before password expires : 7 [student@fedora ~]$ date -d '1970-01-01 + 20737 days' Sun Oct 11 12:00:00 AM EEST 2026

The password itself is never stored, only its hash: the result of a one-way function. It is easy to compute the hash of a password, but there is no way to compute the password from the hash: the only way back is to guess a password, hash it, and compare. The second field of /etc/shadow is made of parts separated by $: Part In the example What it is algorithm y the hash function: y is yescrypt, 6 is SHA-512, 1 is the old MD5 parameters j9T the cost of the algorithm: how much work a hash takes salt Xr3aB7tPq2LkV9sD1fGh0J a random text, different for every user, added to the password before hashing hash 9mQeT4bW1sZx... the hash of the salt and the password note To check a password, login (or sudo, or passwd) reads the algorithm, the parameters and the salt from /etc/shadow, hashes the typed password with them, and compares the result with the stored hash. If they are equal, the password is correct. openssl passwd computes a hash in the same way (-6 is SHA-512): [student@fedora ~]$ openssl passwd -6 -salt Xr3aB7tP pass123 $6$Xr3aB7tP$Z1hKbIRkawX63bJfb3tDz.QpCpVlFdOHOBw1ZdK7Oe/6P0K3E0OUwMhyG7PXhsJPPu.ZobCXoTYNxvAQ3HExk0 [student@fedora ~]$ openssl passwd -6 -salt Xr3aB7tP pass123 $6$Xr3aB7tP$Z1hKbIRkawX63bJfb3tDz.QpCpVlFdOHOBw1ZdK7Oe/6P0K3E0OUwMhyG7PXhsJPPu.ZobCXoTYNxvAQ3HExk0 [student@fedora ~]$ openssl passwd -6 -salt Xr3aB7tP pass124 $6$Xr3aB7tP$msVqpr1xVM/DA2zRy9MVn8yIL5iisMXZpqd3XHD5Ix0aQ5QqD8D3Q91LXVy0w9hPqQLzRYsUVEH5g5oBfNp9// [student@fedora ~]$ openssl passwd -6 -salt Lp0wQ2zM pass123 $6$Lp0wQ2zM$Uo9XUE/86KtNuRc.TcZpxeM0kWUejWZuFOaRQSujvsfACi8WRK55XpaV3Z3WE8TLEWQBF9Jgn4ByzOvO43Ukw0 The same password and the same salt always give the same hash: this is how the password is checked. One different letter gives a completely different hash. The same password with another salt gives another hash: two users with the same password have different lines in /etc/shadow. info Why is the hash not in /etc/passwd, which everyone can read? Because the check works for an attacker too: with a copy of the hash, they can hash one password after another, on their own computer, until one of them gives the same hash. Nobody sees these tries, and nothing slows them down, unlike login, which waits after a wrong password and writes it in the log. A slow algorithm, like yescrypt, makes every try cost more, and the salt makes the attacker start again for every user, but a simple password is still found quickly. That is why only root can read /etc/shadow: the programs that check passwords, login, sudo and passwd, run as root, so they can read it.

Command What it does passwd changes your password; it asks for the old one first sudo passwd <USER> changes the password of another user (only root can do it) sudo passwd -l <USER> locks the password: adds !! (Ubuntu: !) in front of the hash, so no password works sudo passwd -u <USER> unlocks it: removes the !, and the old password works again sudo passwd -S <USER> prints the state of the password: set, locked or empty caution When you type a password in the terminal, nothing appears on the screen. Type it anyway and press Enter. Fedora refuses passwords that are too short or too simple, unless you are root.

A group is a set of users. A group has no rights by itself: a file can give permissions to a group, and sudo trusts one group, and then every member gets these rights. Like a user, a group has a name and a number, the GID (Group ID), and the kernel knows only the number. Every user has: one primary group, the GID in /etc/passwd: the new files of the user get this group. On Fedora and Ubuntu, useradd creates a group with the same name as the user, only for them; any number of supplementary groups, listed in /etc/group, for example wheel. The local groups are kept in /etc/group, one group per line, with 4 fields: [student@fedora ~]$ getent group wheel wheel:x:10:student [student@fedora ~]$ getent group student student:x:1000: Field In the example What it is 1 wheel the name of the group 2 x the password of the group, almost never used 3 10 the GID 4 student the members, separated by ,: the users that have it as a supplementary group caution The users that have a group as their primary group are not listed in its last field: student is the only member of the group student, but the list is empty. Use id <USER> to see all the groups of a user.

When you log in, a process gets the label of your user. On a text terminal, /dev/tty3 for example: systemd starts agetty on the terminal, as root; it prints login: and reads the user name; agetty becomes login (it runs exec), still as root, and it asks for the password; login finds the user with the C library, and checks the password with the hash from /etc/shadow; a child of login sets its GID, its groups and, at the end, its UID to the ones of the user; after that, it can never go back to root; the child changes to the home directory and runs (exec) the shell from /etc/passwd. [student@fedora ~]$ ps -t tty3 -o user,pid,ppid,comm USER PID PPID COMMAND root 5120 1 login student 5191 5120 bash login still runs as root, and waits for the shell to end; the shell runs as student. Every program you start from it inherits this label. A graphical login and ssh do the same steps. info The groups are copied from the groups database only when a process gets the label of a user: at login, and by su and sudo. If you are added to a new group, the processes that are already running do not have it, and neither do their children: a new terminal window is a child of Sway, which got its groups when you logged in. To get the new group, log out and log in again, or, for one shell only, start a login shell with su - student, or run newgrp <GROUP>.

root is the user with the UID 0. For a process whose effective UID is 0, the kernel skips most of its checks: it can read and write any file, send signals to any process, mount disks and change the network. Installing software and adding users need root for the same reason: they write files that belong to root, in /usr and in /etc. The home directory of root is /root, not /home/root, so that root can still log in when /home is on another disk that does not work. The kernel looks only at the number: root is just the name of the UID 0, usually on the first line of /etc/passwd. Two user names with the same UID are the same user for the kernel: this is how an attacker can hide a second root. danger A mistake as root can destroy the whole system: root gets no Permission denied to stop it. Work as a regular user, and become root only for the commands that need it.

sudo runs one command as root. It asks for your password, not the one of root, and it lets you do it only if you are an administrator. A user is an administrator if they are a member of one special group, whose name depends on the distribution: Distribution The group of the administrators Fedora, Red Hat, CentOS wheel Ubuntu, Debian, Linux Mint sudo To make a user an administrator, add them to this group; to take the right away, remove them from it (see Managing Users and Groups). student is in wheel, so it may use sudo: [student@fedora ~]$ cat /etc/shadow cat: /etc/shadow: Permission denied [student@fedora ~]$ sudo whoami [sudo] password for student: root [student@fedora ~]$ sudo whoami root sudo itself runs as root, and it starts the command as root too: whoami prints root. It remembers the password for 5 minutes, in this terminal: the second sudo did not ask for it. A user who is not an administrator gets bob is not in the sudoers file., and the command does not start. sudo writes every command in the system log: who ran what, as whom, and from which directory. [student@fedora ~]$ sudo journalctl -t sudo | tail -2 Oct 27 10:02:11 fedora sudo[3311]: student : TTY=pts/0 ; PWD=/home/student ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/bin/whoami Oct 27 10:02:20 fedora sudo[3315]: student : TTY=pts/0 ; PWD=/home/student ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/bin/journalctl -t sudo While the command runs, sudo does not go away: it waits for the command to end and passes on the signals that it receives. On Fedora, sudo also runs the command in a new pseudo terminal of its own (the option use_pty, see Terminal Emulators in lab 04), so there are two sudo processes: the first one stays on your terminal, the second one opens the new pseudo terminal and starts the command in it. With sudo sleep 300 running in a shell with the PID 2817: [student@fedora ~]$ pstree -pu 2817 bash(2817)───sudo(3320,root)───sudo(3321)───sleep(3322) [student@fedora ~]$ ps -o pid,ppid,tty,comm -p 3320,3321,3322 PID PPID TT COMMAND 3320 2817 pts/0 sudo 3321 3320 pts/2 sudo 3322 3321 pts/2 sleep pstree -p shows the PIDs, and -u the user, where it changes: sudo runs as root, and so does everything under it. The second sudo and sleep are on pts/2, not on pts/0: ps -t pts/0 does not show the command started with sudo. Find it with pstree, pgrep or the PPID instead. info The new pseudo terminal protects you: a program started with sudo cannot type commands into your own terminal after it ends. Some distributions do not use it (sudo 1.9.14 and later use it by default); there, pstree shows only one sudo. Command What it does sudo <command> runs command as root sudo -u <USER> <command> runs the command as another user; it asks for your password, not theirs sudo -i starts a login shell of root, in /root, with the variables of root sudo -s starts a shell as root, in the current directory sudo -E <command> keeps your environment variables, except PATH; without it, sudo removes most of them sudo -l lists what you are allowed to run sudo -k forgets the password: the next sudo asks again sudo !! runs the previous command again, with sudo: bash replaces !! before sudo starts info The group of the administrators is chosen in the settings of sudo, the file /etc/sudoers. You do not need to change it, or to understand it, in this lab: you only add users to the group, or remove them from it. If you are curious, the line %wheel ALL=(ALL) ALL near its end is the one that gives the group wheel its rights.

su (switch user) starts a shell as another user, and asks for the password of that user: Command What it does su - <USER> starts a login shell of the user: their home directory, variables and groups su - the same, for root; it asks for the password of root exit leaves the shell, back to your own [student@fedora ~]$ su - Password: su: Authentication failure [student@fedora ~]$ sudo -i [root@fedora ~]# whoami root [root@fedora ~]# exit logout [student@fedora ~]$ On Fedora and on Ubuntu, root usually has no password (it is locked in /etc/shadow), unless you set one when you installed the system: su - does not work, and sudo -i is the way to get a shell of root. With su, everybody who becomes root has to know the same password, and the log cannot tell who it was; with sudo, everyone uses their own. tip The prompt shows # instead of $ in a shell of root. Leave it with exit as soon as you are done.

sudo runs the command, not the whole line. The redirects are done by your shell, which runs as you, before sudo starts: [student@fedora ~]$ sudo echo "192.168.1.20 printer" >> /etc/hosts bash: /etc/hosts: Permission denied [student@fedora ~]$ echo "192.168.1.20 printer" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts 192.168.1.20 printer In the first line, bash tries to open /etc/hosts for >>, as student, and fails: sudo echo never starts. In the second line, tee runs as root: it reads the text from the pipe and writes it into the file and on the screen. -a (append) adds it at the end, like >>; without it, tee replaces the content of the file, like >. tip tee also prints the text on the screen. To hide it, send its output to /dev/null: echo "192.168.1.20 printer" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts > /dev/null. This redirect is also done by your shell, as you, but it works because of the permissions of /dev/null: they are rw-rw-rw- (666), so every user may write to it.

The commands below change /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow and /etc/group for you, so they need sudo: Command What it does sudo useradd -m <USER> creates a user, with a group of the same name; -m creates the home directory, -c sets the full name, -s the shell sudo passwd <USER> sets the password of the user sudo groupadd <GROUP> creates a group sudo usermod -aG <GROUP> <USER> adds the user to a supplementary group sudo usermod <OPTIONS> <USER> changes a user that already exists; it takes most of the options of useradd: -c the full name, -s the shell, ... sudo gpasswd -a <USER> <GROUP> also adds the user to the group sudo gpasswd -d <USER> <GROUP> removes the user from the group sudo userdel -r <USER> deletes the user; -r also deletes its home directory sudo groupdel <GROUP> deletes a group; it refuses if the group is the primary group of a user [student@fedora ~]$ sudo useradd -m -c "Dave Brown" dave [student@fedora ~]$ sudo passwd dave New password: Retype new password: passwd: password updated successfully [student@fedora ~]$ sudo usermod -aG students dave [student@fedora ~]$ id dave uid=1003(dave) gid=1004(dave) groups=1004(dave),1003(students) [student@fedora ~]$ ls -ld /home/dave drwx------. 3 dave dave 80 Oct 27 10:15 /home/dave The numbers may be different on your computer: useradd takes the next free UID and GID. A new user is not an administrator. sudo works for student because student is in wheel; dave is not, so sudo refuses him, even with his correct password: [student@fedora ~]$ su - dave Password: [dave@fedora ~]$ sudo whoami [sudo] password for dave: dave is not in the sudoers file. [dave@fedora ~]$ exit logout [student@fedora ~]$ sudo usermod -aG wheel dave [student@fedora ~]$ su - dave Password: [dave@fedora ~]$ sudo whoami [sudo] password for dave: root [dave@fedora ~]$ exit logout [student@fedora ~]$ sudo gpasswd -d dave wheel Removing user dave from group wheel The first sudo fails: dave is not in wheel, the group of the administrators. The attempt is still written in the log. After he is added to wheel, a new login (su - dave) has the new group, and sudo works, with his own password. gpasswd -d takes the right away again. danger Never forget the -a of usermod -aG. usermod -G students dave replaces all the supplementary groups of dave with students. Run it on yourself and you lose wheel, and with it sudo. usermod changes the fields of /etc/passwd for you, and userdel removes the user, with their group and, with -r, their home directory: [student@fedora ~]$ sudo usermod -c "David Brown" dave [student@fedora ~]$ getent passwd dave dave:x:1003:1004:David Brown:/home/dave:/bin/bash [student@fedora ~]$ sudo userdel -r dave [student@fedora ~]$ id dave id: 'dave': no such user [student@fedora ~]$ ls -d /home/dave ls: cannot access '/home/dave': No such file or directory userdel refuses to delete a user who is still logged in, or has processes running: it prints userdel: user dave is currently used by process 4321. Log the user out first.

Every file and directory has one owner (a user), one group, and three sets of permissions: for the owner (u, user), for the group (g) and for all the others (o). The owner and the group are kept as numbers, a UID and a GID, and they are independent: the owner does not have to be a member of the group. ls -l shows them: [student@fedora lab05]$ ls -l notes.txt -rw-r-----. 1 student students 9 Oct 27 10:20 notes.txt Part In the example What it is type - - a file, d a directory, l a symbolic link, c and b devices u rw- the owner, student, can read and write the file g r-- the members of the group students can only read it o --- everybody else can do nothing owner student the user that owns the file, usually the one that created it group students the group of the file, usually the primary group of the one that created it stat prints the same information, in the format you ask for: [student@fedora lab05]$ stat -c '%A %a %U %G %n' notes.txt /etc/passwd /etc/shadow -rw-r----- 640 student students notes.txt -rw-r--r-- 644 root root /etc/passwd ---------- 0 root root /etc/shadow %A are the permissions as letters, %a as a number (see chmod), %U the owner, %G the group and %n the name.

The same letters have a different meaning for files and for directories: Permission Value For a file For a directory r read 4 read the content (cat, less) list the names of the files inside (ls); ls -l also needs x, as it reads each file's details, which means "entering" the directory | w write | 2 | change the content | create, delete and rename the files inside, only together with x, as it needs to enter the directory first | | x execute | 1 | run it as a program | enter it (cd) and reach the files inside, if you know their names | A directory is a file whose content is a list of names, each pointing to a file. r reads this list, w changes it, and x uses it to reach a file. This has two consequences: creating, renaming or deleting a file is a change of the directory, not of the file: with w on a directory you can delete a file that you cannot even read; to reach a file, you need x on every directory of its path: cat /home/student/lab05/notes.txt needs x on /, /home, /home/student and /home/student/lab05. [student@fedora lab05]$ ls -ld noread noenter d--x------. 2 student student 60 Oct 27 10:20 noread dr--------. 2 student student 60 Oct 27 10:20 noenter [student@fedora lab05]$ ls noread ls: cannot open directory 'noread': Permission denied [student@fedora lab05]$ cat noread/secret.txt top secret [student@fedora lab05]$ ls noenter ls: cannot access 'noenter/secret.txt': Permission denied secret.txt [student@fedora lab05]$ cd noenter bash: cd: noenter: Permission denied noread has x but no r: its names cannot be listed, but a file whose name you know can be opened. noenter has r but no x: ls can read the names, but not reach the files to show them; cd cannot enter it. info On Fedora, the home directories are drwx------: the other users cannot even enter yours, so they cannot reach your files, whatever their permissions. On Ubuntu, they are drwxr-x---: the members of your primary group may also list and enter it, but this group usually has no other member. An older Ubuntu, or one upgraded from an older version, may still have drwxr-xr-x, open to everybody: check yours with ls -ld ~.

The kernel checks the label of the process in this order, and the first match decides: if the UID of the process is 0, root: everything is allowed (except running a file without any x); if the UID is the owner of the file: the u permissions are used; if one of the groups of the process is the group of the file: the g permissions are used; otherwise: the o permissions are used. For notes.txt above, -rw-r----- student students: Process run by Its groups Uses Read Write root root - yes yes student student, wheel u yes yes bob bob, students g yes no carol carol o no no caution Only one set is used. With ----rw----, the owner can do nothing, even if they are in the group: the owner already matched at step 2, so the g permissions are never checked.

chmod (change mode) changes the permissions. Only the owner of the file (or root) can run it. The permissions can be written with letters: Part Letters who u the owner, g the group, o the others (not the owner and not a member of the group), a all three | how | + adds, - removes, = sets exactly these | | what | r, w, x | Command What it does chmod u+x script.sh adds x for the owner chmod g+w,o-r notes.txt adds w for the group and removes r for the others chmod go-rwx notes.txt removes everything for the group and the others chmod a=r readme.txt sets r-- for everybody chmod -R g+rX project for the group, adds r to project and everything inside, and x only to the directories and to the files that are already executable for someone | chmod u=rw,go=r notes.txt | sets exactly rw- for the user and r-- for the group and others (rw-r--r--); = replaces the old permissions instead of adding to them | or with numbers, in octal: r is 4, w is 2 and x is 1. Add them for each of u, g and o: Letters u g o Number rw-r----- 4 + 2 = 6 4 = 4 0 640 rwxr-xr-x 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 4 + 1 = 5 4 + 1 = 5 755 rw-r--r-- 6 4 4 644 rw------- 6 0 0 600 [student@fedora lab05]$ ls -l myid.sh -rw-r--r--. 1 student student 18 Oct 27 10:20 myid.sh [student@fedora lab05]$ ./myid.sh bash: ./myid.sh: Permission denied [student@fedora lab05]$ chmod u+x myid.sh [student@fedora lab05]$ ./myid.sh student [student@fedora lab05]$ chmod 600 myid.sh [student@fedora lab05]$ ls -l myid.sh -rw-------. 1 student student 18 Oct 27 10:20 myid.sh tip Use the letters to change some permissions and keep the others (chmod g+w), and the numbers to set all of them at once (chmod 640). With -R, use the letters: chmod -R 644 box also removes the x of the directories, and then nobody can enter them, not even chmod; chmod -R u=rwX,go=rX box gives the files rw-r--r-- and the directories rwxr-xr-x.

New files do not get all the permissions: the program that creates them asks for rw-rw-rw- (666) for a file and rwxrwxrwx (777) for a directory, and the kernel removes the bits of the umask of the process. umask is a built-in command of the shell (help umask), and every process inherits it from its parent. [student@fedora lab05]$ umask 0022 [student@fedora lab05]$ touch new.txt [student@fedora lab05]$ mkdir newdir [student@fedora lab05]$ ls -ld new.txt newdir -rw-r--r--. 1 student student 0 Oct 27 10:25 new.txt drwxr-xr-x. 2 student student 40 Oct 27 10:25 newdir File Directory the program asks for 666 rw-rw-rw- 777 rwxrwxrwx umask 022 removes 022 ----w--w- 022 ----w--w- the result 644 rw-r--r-- 755 rwxr-xr-x 022 removes w for the group and for the others. A new file is never executable: umask can only remove bits, and programs do not ask for x for files. umask 077 makes every new file private: 600 for files and 700 for directories. It lasts until the shell ends. info Some systems use umask 002 for the regular users: then the new files are rw-rw-r--. This is safe because every user has a primary group of their own, with no other members.

Command What it does sudo chown bob notes.txt the owner becomes bob sudo chown bob:students notes.txt the owner becomes bob and the group students chown :students notes.txt only the group, like chgrp chgrp students notes.txt only the group chown -R, chgrp -R the directory and everything inside it sudo chown 1005 notes.txt the owner becomes the UID 1005, even if there is not user with UID 1005 Only root can give a file to another user: otherwise, anyone could fill the disk of another user, or hide what they did. The owner can change the group of a file, but only to one of the groups of their process. [student@fedora lab05]$ chown carol notes.txt chown: changing ownership of 'notes.txt': Operation not permitted [student@fedora lab05]$ sudo chown carol notes.txt [student@fedora lab05]$ ls -l notes.txt -rw-r-----. 1 carol students 9 Oct 27 10:20 notes.txt

There are three more bits, shown by ls -l in the place of an x: Bit Number ls -l shows On a program On a directory setuid 4000 -rwsr-xr-x runs with the effective UID of the owner of the file ignored setgid 2000 -rwxr-sr-x, drwxrwsr-x runs with the effective GID of the group of the file new files get the group of the directory; new directories also get the bit sticky 1000 drwxrwxrwt ignored a file can be deleted or renamed only by its owner, the owner of the directory and root With letters, they are u+s, g+s and +t; with numbers, the 4th digit in front: chmod 2775 project is rwxrwsr-x. A capital S or T means that the bit is set, but the x under it is not.

passwd must write your new hash into /etc/shadow, which only root can change. /usr/bin/passwd belongs to root and has the setuid bit: whoever starts it, the process runs as root. [student@fedora ~]$ ls -l /usr/bin/passwd /usr/bin/sudo /usr/bin/su -rwsr-xr-x. 1 root root 32648 Jul 24 03:00 /usr/bin/passwd -rwsr-xr-x. 1 root root 56920 Jul 24 03:00 /usr/bin/su ---s--x--x. 1 root root 262536 Jul 24 03:00 /usr/bin/sudo When a program with the setuid bit starts, the kernel changes two of its credentials: the effective and the saved UID become the owner of the file, root. The real UID stays the one of the user who started it. Run passwd in one terminal (do not type anything), and look at it from another one: [student@fedora ~]$ ps -o pid,ruser,euser,suser,comm -C passwd PID RUSER EUSER SUSER COMMAND 6011 student root root passwd The kernel checks the effective UID, so passwd may write /etc/shadow. passwd reads the real UID to find out who started it, so it changes only your password. The Saved UID​ A careful setuid program does not work as root all the time: it works as you, and uses root only for the few steps that need it, so that a bug in the rest of it can only do what you could do anyway. The saved UID makes this possible. After the exec, the Uid: line of the program is 1000 0 0 0: the program sets its effective UID to its real one, 1000 (Uid: 1000 1000 0 1000): root stays only in the saved UID; when it needs root again, it sets its effective UID back to 0 (Uid: 1000 0 0 0): this is allowed, because 0 is its saved UID; when it does not need root any more, it sets all three UIDs to 1000 (Uid: 1000 1000 1000 1000): 0 is none of its UIDs now, so it can never go back. danger Never add +s to a program that belongs to root: it runs as root for everybody, and one bug in it makes anybody root. A setuid copy of bash gives a shell of root to every user. Leave the setuid bit to the programs that are made for it: passwd, su, sudo. info The kernel ignores the setuid and the setgid bit on scripts, like myid.sh. A script does not run by itself: the kernel starts the program on its first line, /bin/bash, and gives it the script to read. A bash with the label of root would be dangerous, because the user who starts it can change what it does, for example with environment variables. So the bits work only for compiled programs, like passwd.

When several users work in the same directory, the new files should belong to the group of the project, not to the primary group of each user. The setgid bit on a directory does this: [student@fedora ~]$ sudo mkdir /srv/project [student@fedora ~]$ sudo chgrp students /srv/project [student@fedora ~]$ sudo chmod 2775 /srv/project [student@fedora ~]$ ls -ld /srv/project drwxrwsr-x. 2 root students 40 Oct 27 10:40 /srv/project [student@fedora ~]$ sudo -u bob touch /srv/project/bob.txt [student@fedora ~]$ ls -l /srv/project total 0 -rw-r--r--. 1 bob students 0 Oct 27 10:41 bob.txt bob.txt belongs to bob, but its group is students, the group of the directory, not bob.

/tmp must be writable by everyone, so everyone has w on it. Without anything else, anyone could delete the files of the others. The sticky bit, t, allows deleting or renaming a file in the directory only to the owner of the file, the owner of the directory and root: [student@fedora ~]$ ls -ld /tmp drwxrwxrwt. 21 root root 520 Oct 27 10:00 /tmp tip find can look for the special bits: find /usr -perm -4000 prints the files that have at least the setuid bit.

The prompt of bash is built from the shell variable PS1 (see lab 04). On Fedora, it is [\u@\h \W]\$ (on Ubuntu, \u@\h:\w\$ , with colors): Escape Meaning For student For root \u the user student root \h the host name fedora fedora \W the name of the current directory (\w is the whole path) lab05 ~ \$ $ for the users, # for the UID 0 $ # The prompt is only text, and any user can change it: [student@fedora ~]$ PS1='[root@fedora \W]# ' [root@fedora ~]# whoami student [root@fedora ~]# cat /etc/shadow cat: /etc/shadow: Permission denied caution Do not trust the prompt to tell you who you are. whoami and id ask the kernel for the label of the process.

PS1 can hold any text, and these escapes (man bash, section PROMPTING): Escape Replaced with \u, \h the user; the host name, up to the first . \w, \W the whole path of the current directory, with ~ for your home; only its last name \$ $, or # if the effective UID is 0 \t, \A the time, as HH:MM:SS and HH:MM \d the date, like Tue Oct 27 \j the number of jobs of the shell (lab 04) \n a new line \e the escape character, which starts a color code \[, \] put around a color code: it takes no space on the screen [student@fedora lab05]$ PS1='\A \u in \w \$ ' 10:52 student in ~/lab05 $ PS1='[\u@\h \W]\$ ' [student@fedora lab05]$ The colors are written as \e[<code>m: 31 red, 32 green, 33 yellow, 34 blue, 1; in front makes them bold, and 0 goes back to normal. The \[ and \] around them tell bash that they take no space on the screen; without them, long commands are drawn over the prompt. PS1='\[\e[1;32m\]\u@\h\[\e[0m\]:\[\e[1;34m\]\w\[\e[0m\]\$ ' tip A change of PS1 lasts until the shell ends. To keep it, add the line PS1='...' at the end of ~/.bashrc; bash reads it when it starts (source ~/.bashrc reads it now). root has its own /root/.bashrc, so you can give the shells of root a red prompt, that you cannot miss.

Problem Solution Permission denied on a file ls -l the file and id: find which set applies to you (owner, group or others) and what it allows Permission denied on a file that has r for you One of the directories of its path has no x for you: ls -ld each of them ./script.sh: Permission denied The file has no x: chmod u+x script.sh Operation not permitted for chmod or chown Only the owner may run chmod, and only root may change the owner: use sudo student is not in the sudoers file. The user is not an administrator: not in wheel (Fedora) or sudo (Ubuntu); an administrator must run sudo usermod -aG wheel student, then log in again sudo echo ... > file: Permission denied The redirect is done by your shell, before sudo: use echo ... | sudo tee file su: Authentication failure for su - root has no password on Fedora and Ubuntu: use sudo -i A new group does not show up in id The groups are read at login: log in again, or start a new login shell with su - <USER> usermod -G removed my groups You forgot -a; add them back with sudo usermod -aG <GROUP> <USER> passwd: BAD PASSWORD: The password is shorter than 8 characters Choose a longer, less simple password useradd: user 'bob' already exists The user is already there: check with id bob userdel: user bob is currently used by process 1234 bob still has processes: end them, or log bob out first rm: remove write-protected regular file? You do not have w on the file, but you have it on the directory: answer y to delete it anyway rm: cannot remove ... Operation not permitted in /tmp The sticky bit: only the owner of the file can delete it A file shows a number instead of an owner in ls -l The user was deleted, but the file still has its UID

The exercises get harder as you go: 🧪 First Steps (exercises 1 - 27) goes once through everything in this lab: each exercise shows one command or one idea, in a few short steps, to do in the lab; 🏠 Going Further (exercises 28 - 51) has longer exercises to do at home: each one starts with a goal, a situation to solve or a question to answer, and puts together several commands; 📝 Challenges (exercises 52 - 60) has the hardest ones. Exercise 1 creates the files that all the other exercises start from, and exercises 2 - 3 ask you to create the users, the group and the shared directory used by the rest of the lab. Run the commands in ~/lab05, unless the exercise says otherwise. If you change or delete one of the files from exercise 1, run its commands again to get it back. In exercises 2 - 3 you create two more users, bob and carol, with the password uso2026, and the group students, with bob as its only member. In the exercises, student plays the owner of the files, bob a member of their group, and carol one of the others. Your home directory is closed to the other users, so the files that they must reach are in /srv/lab05. The checks give the values of the lab computers, with Fedora. If you work at home on Ubuntu, some of them are different, as shown in Fedora and Ubuntu: for example, the group of the administrators is sudo instead of wheel.

The exercises do not tell you the exact commands and options: they tell you what to do, and a 💡 hint tells you where to look. Most of the time you know the command from the lab, and you have to find the option in its manual page, as explained in Searching in a Manual Page in lab 02: open man <command>, type / and the word from the hint, and press n until you find it. When you do not know the command, search the short descriptions of all the manual pages with man -k: [student@fedora ~]$ man -k 'group' chgrp (1) - change group ownership gpasswd (1) - administer /etc/group and /etc/gshadow groupadd (8) - create a new group groupdel (8) - delete a group ... Where to look For man -k <word> a command whose description has <word> man <command>, then /<word> an option of the command help <command> the built-in commands of bash, like umask man ps, /STANDARD FORMAT the names of the columns for ps -o, for example the users and groups of a process man 5 proc, /status the lines of /proc/<PID>/status, for example Uid: and Groups: Many exercises ask you to inspect the credentials of a process: its real and effective user, its groups. Use the two ways from The Credentials of a Process: ps -o with the right columns, and the Uid:, Gid: and Groups: lines of /proc/<PID>/status. Keep two terminals side by side: one to start the process, one to inspect it. danger Use sudo only where the exercise asks for it. Do not change the permissions or the owner of anything outside ~/lab05, /srv/lab05 and /srv/project: sudo chmod -R or sudo chown -R on a directory of the system can break it for good. Never remove yourself (student) from the group of the administrators, wheel on Fedora and sudo on Ubuntu, or you lose sudo.

Do these exercises in order, during the lab. Each one starts with what it wants you to achieve, and tries one command, or one idea, from the lab: read the section linked at the end of the exercise if you get stuck. The practice tree: Create the files and directories that the other exercises use, in ~/lab05. run these commands to create the files used in the exercises (copy them from the browser with Ctrl+C and paste them in the terminal with Ctrl+Shift+V): mkdir -p ~/lab05/box ~/lab05/noread ~/lab05/noenter cd ~/lab05 printf 'buy milk
' > notes.txt printf 'my first box
' > box/item.txt printf 'top secret
' > noread/secret.txt printf 'top secret
' > noenter/secret.txt printf '#!/bin/bash
id -un
' > myid.sh show the tree of ~/lab05. Check: ~/lab05 has the directories box, noread and noenter, and the files myid.sh, notes.txt, box/item.txt and the two secret.txt. → Navigation Creating the users Two new users and a group: Create bob and carol, the two users who play a member of your group and a stranger in the rest of the lab, and the group students, with bob as its only member. check that bob and carol do not exist yet; create the user bob, with a home directory, the shell /bin/bash and the full name Bob Jones, and the user carol, with a home directory, the shell /bin/bash and the full name Carol White; set the password of both of them to uso2026; create the group students, and add bob to it, as a supplementary group, without removing his other groups; print the labels of bob and carol, the line of students from the groups database, and the owners of the directories in /home. 💡 man useradd: search for home, shell and comment (the full name is the GECOS field); Fedora gives a new user /bin/bash anyway, but Ubuntu gives /bin/sh. man -k group finds the command that creates a group; in man usermod, search for -G and then for append. Check: before, no such user; after, bob and carol have the next free UIDs (1001 and 1002) and a group of their own each, and they own /home/bob and /home/carol; students lists only bob. Setting the password may warn BAD PASSWORD: The password is shorter than 8 characters, but root may set it anyway. → Managing Users and Groups · Groups A shared directory: Prepare /srv/lab05, the directory where bob and carol will try to reach your files, since they cannot enter your home directory. create /srv/lab05 as root; make yourself its owner and students its group, with one command; create in it, as yourself, the file plan.txt, with the text the plan, and report.txt, with the text the report; give report.txt the group students and the permissions rw-r-----; list the directory itself, then its content. 💡 chown and chgrp: man chown, search for OWNER:GROUP. You are not a member of students, so changing the group needs root too. man ls: search for directory to list the directory itself. Check: /srv/lab05 is drwxr-xr-x student students; report.txt is -rw-r----- student students and plan.txt is -rw-r--r-- (-rw-rw-r-- on Ubuntu, because of the umask) with your own group. → Owner, Group and Permissions Users Who am I: Find out which user and which groups the kernel sees for your shell, and for the other users. print your user name, with two different commands; print your whole label, then only your UID, then only the names of your groups; print the labels of bob, carol and root, without logging in as them; print the lines of the group of the administrators (wheel, or sudo on Ubuntu), of students and of student from the groups database. 💡 man id: search for name, user and groups; getent reads the groups database too. Check: the name is student, the UID 1000; your groups are student and the group of the administrators (Ubuntu: sudo, and a few more); root has the UID 0, and bob is also in students. The group of the administrators lists student, but student lists nobody: a user is not listed in its primary group. → Who Am I · Groups The credentials of your shell: See all the credentials that the kernel keeps for your shell, and learn the two ways to read them. print the PID of your shell; print its real user, its effective user, its saved user and its supplementary groups, with one ps command; print the Uid:, Gid: and Groups: lines of its status file in /proc; find out, in the manual, what each of the 4 numbers of Uid: is. 💡 $$ is the PID of the shell (lab 04); man ps, section STANDARD FORMAT SPECIFIERS: search for real user, effective user, saved user and supplementary; man 5 proc: search for Uid. Check: the real, the effective and the saved user are all student; Uid: has 4 times 1000: real, effective, saved and file system UID; Groups: has 10 and 1000, the GIDs of wheel and student (on Ubuntu, 27 for sudo, and the GIDs of your other groups). → The Credentials of a Process The users of the processes: Find out which users run the processes of the system, and how many processes each of them has. list the processes of your terminal, with their user and UID; count the processes of every user of the system; find the two users with the most processes. 💡 man ps: search for every process and for user; count them with sort and uniq (lab 03). Check: the processes of your terminal run as student; root and student have the most processes. → The User of a Process · Pipes The users database The users database: Read your own account in the users database, look up other users by name and by UID, and find out how many users exist only to run services. print the permissions of /etc/passwd, and your line, once from the file and once from the users database; find in it your UID, your home directory and your shell; find the users with the UIDs 0 and 65534, and print the line of bob; count all the users, and the users whose shell is nologin; print the UID limits for the regular and the system users. 💡 man getent: the DATABASES are passwd, group, shadow, ...; man grep: search for count; man login.defs: search for UID_MIN. Check: everyone can read /etc/passwd; your line has 7 fields, student:x:1000:1000:...:/home/student:/bin/bash; 0 is root, 65534 is nobody; there are a few dozen users, and most of them have nologin: they are the system users, with a UID below 1000. → /etc/passwd · getent · UID Ranges Passwords /etc/shadow: See where the passwords are kept, who may read them, how a password is stored, and when it was last changed. print the permissions of /etc/shadow, then try to print it; print your line and the line of bob, and find the algorithm of your hash; print the password dates of your account; turn the third field of your line into a date. 💡 man 5 shadow explains the fields; man 5 crypt lists the algorithms (search for yescrypt); man chage: search for list; man date: search for --date (the date can be 1970-01-01 + N days). Check: /etc/shadow is ---------- (Ubuntu: -rw-r----- root shadow), and you cannot read it; your hash starts with $y$, yescrypt; steps 3 and 4 give the same date: the day you last set your password (or installed the system). → /etc/shadow Hash a password: See how a hash depends on the password and on the salt. With openssl: hash the password pass123 with SHA-512 and the salt abc, twice; hash it again with the salt xyz; hash pass124 with the salt abc. 💡 man openssl-passwd: search for SHA512 and for salt. Check: the first two hashes are the same; with another salt, or one different letter, the hash is completely different. → Hashes and Salt Who runs passwd: See what the setuid bit of passwd changes in the credentials of the process. in the second terminal, start passwd, and do not type anything; in the first terminal, find its PID, and print its real, its effective and its saved user; print the Uid: line of its status file, and compare it with the one of your shell: which of the UIDs changed? end passwd with Ctrl+C. 💡 man ps: search for command name, to select a process by its name instead of its PID. Check: the real user is student, the effective and the saved user are root; Uid: is 1000 0 0 0. The s bit of /usr/bin/passwd changed the effective and the saved UID, but not the real one: passwd still knows who started it. → setuid · The Credentials of a Process Logging in Log in as bob: Follow a real login on a text terminal, and see which process runs as which user. switch to the third virtual terminal and log in as bob; print the user, the current directory and the label of the shell; go back to Sway (at home, to your graphical desktop), and list the processes of tty3 with their user, real user, PID, PPID and name; print the supplementary groups of the shell of bob, with ps; go back to tty3, and log out. 💡 Ctrl+Alt+F3 (Host+F3 in VirtualBox), and back with Ctrl+Alt+F1 or F2; man ps: search for Select by, to see all the ways to choose the processes, and find the one for a terminal. Check: the shell runs as bob, in /home/bob, with the groups bob and students; login runs as root and is the parent of the bash of bob. → Logging In · Virtual Terminals Becoming root sudo: Run commands as root with sudo, and see how it remembers your password, what it allows you to do and what it writes in the log. print your user and your label as root; do it again, and see that the password is not asked; make sudo forget the password, and try once more; list what you are allowed to run with sudo; 5. try to print the first line of /etc/shadow as yourself; then run the same command again as root, without typing the command again; print the last 5 commands that were run with sudo, from the system log; (optional) print the end of /etc/sudoers as root, and find the line that mentions the group of the administrators (%wheel, or %sudo on Ubuntu); you do not have to understand the rest of the file. 💡 man sudo: search for invalidate and for list; man bash: search for HISTORY EXPANSION and then for !!; man journalctl: search for identifier. Check: the user is root, uid=0(root); after the password is forgotten, it is asked again; the list ends with (ALL) ALL (Ubuntu: (ALL : ALL) ALL): as an administrator, you may run any command, as any user. bash prints the command that !! became, then runs it. The log shows your commands, with your user, your terminal and the directory. → sudo su and sudo: Become another user, or root, in a new shell, with su and with sudo, and see the difference. become bob with su, with a login shell; print the user and the current directory; leave; try to become root with su; start a login shell of root with sudo, print the user and the current directory, and leave it. 💡 man su: search for login; man sudo: search for login too. Check: su asks for the password of bob and starts in /home/bob; su to root fails with Authentication failure (unless root has a password); the shell of root starts in /root, with a # in the prompt. → su The redirect trap: Write into a file of root, and see why putting sudo in front of echo is not enough. create the empty file /srv/lab05/root.txt as root, and look at its owner; add the line hello at its end with sudo echo and >>; find a way that works, with a command that writes to a file and to the screen. 💡 man tee: search for append. Check: step 2 fails with Permission denied, because your shell opens the file; at the end, the file has hello. → The Redirect Trap Which commands need root: Learn to tell which actions need root, before you run them. Before you run them, guess which of these commands need root. Then run them without sudo, check your guesses, and run again with sudo only the ones that failed because of the permissions: touch ~/a.txt and touch /tmp/my.data; cat /etc/passwd and cat /etc/shadow; touch /etc/test.conf; ip address show; ls /root; systemctl restart systemd-resolved; at the end, delete the three files you created. Check: reading /etc/passwd, showing the network and writing in your home directory or in /tmp are allowed to everybody; /etc/shadow, writing in /etc, /root and restarting a service need root. systemctl may ask for your password in a window, instead of failing. → The root User · sudo Managing users and groups Create a user: Create a new account, dave, see when it becomes usable, and see that a new user cannot use sudo. create the user dave, with a home directory, the shell /bin/bash and the full name Dave Brown; print his line from the users database and his line from /etc/shadow; give him a password, and print his line from /etc/shadow again; print his label and the permissions of his home directory, and try to list what is inside it; become dave, with a login shell, and try to print your user as root, with the password of dave; leave, and find the attempt of dave in the log of sudo. 💡 man useradd: search for home, shell and comment. Check: before step 3, the password field in /etc/shadow is ! or !!: nobody can log in as dave yet; after it, the field is a hash that starts with $y$. dave has the next free UID and a group dave of his own; /home/dave is drwx------ (Ubuntu: drwxr-x---), and you are neither dave nor in his group, so you cannot list it. sudo refuses dave: dave is not in the sudoers file., because he is not in the group of the administrators; the log has a line for dave with user NOT in sudoers. → Managing Users and Groups · /etc/shadow · sudo Change a user: Change an existing account, its full name and its shell, and see which fields of /etc/passwd change. After each step, print the line of dave from the users database, and find the field that changed: change the full name of dave to David Brown; change his shell to /usr/sbin/nologin, and try to become dave with su; give him back the shell /bin/bash, and become dave again; leave his shell. 💡 man usermod: search for comment and for shell. Check: the 5th field becomes David Brown, the 7th /usr/sbin/nologin; with this shell, su fails with This account is currently not available., even with the right password; with /bin/bash, it works again. → Managing Users and Groups · /etc/passwd Groups of a user: Add a user to a group and remove him from it, with the two commands that can do it, and create and delete a group. After each step, print the groups of dave: add dave to students, without removing his other groups; create the group tas, and add dave to it, this time with the command that administers a group; remove dave from students, with the same command; delete the group tas. 💡 man usermod: search for append; man gpasswd: search for add and for delete; man -k group finds the command that deletes a group. Check: dave is in dave and students, then also in tas, then only in dave and tas, and at the end only in dave; getent group tas prints nothing. → Managing Users and Groups · Groups Delete a user: Delete an account completely: the user, his group and his home directory. in the second terminal, become dave with a login shell; in the first terminal, try to delete dave; leave the shell of dave, and delete him together with his home directory; check that the user dave, the group dave and /home/dave are all gone. 💡 man userdel: search for home. Check: while dave is logged in, userdel refuses: user dave is currently used by process ...; at the end, id dave prints no such user, getent group dave prints nothing, and /home/dave does not exist. → Managing Users and Groups File permissions Read the permissions: Learn to read who owns a file, and what each user may do with it. print the permissions, the owner and the group of notes.txt, /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow and /usr/bin/ls, and of the directories /tmp and ~ (not their content); print the same with stat, as letters and as numbers, with the owner, the group and the name. 💡 man stat: search for %a, %A, %U, %G and --format. Check: for each file, say who the owner is and what the owner, the group and the others can do; ~ is drwx------ (700) on Fedora, drwxr-x--- (750) on Ubuntu. → Owner, Group and Permissions chmod: Change the permissions one at a time, with letters, or all at once, with a number, and see that a program needs x to run. on notes.txt, remove r for the group and the others; remove w for yourself, and try to add a line to it; add w back, and add the line; set the permissions of notes.txt back to rw-r--r-- with one command, with letters; run ./myid.sh; give it rwxr-xr-x, with a number, and run it again; give myid.sh the permissions rw-------, with a number, and try to run it. Check: after step 1, notes.txt is -rw-------; in step 2 your own shell gets Permission denied; after step 3 it is -rw-r--r-- again. Without x, ./myid.sh gives Permission denied; with 755, it prints student; with 600, it is denied again. → chmod r and x for directories: See what r and x allow on a directory, one without the other. give noread only x for you (--x------) and noenter only r (r--------); try to list them, to enter them, and to print the secret.txt inside them; give both of them back rwxr-xr-x. Check: noread cannot be listed, but noread/secret.txt can be printed; noenter lists the name with an error, but cannot be entered and its file cannot be printed. The error comes from the colors of ls, which need the details of the file: \ls noenter lists the name without it.→ r, w and x Who can read the report: See which of the three sets of permissions applies to the owner, to a member of the group and to the others. /srv/lab05/report.txt is rw-r----- student students. print it as yourself, as bob and as carol; try to add a line to it as bob. 💡 man sudo: search for -u user to run a command as another user (it asks for your password); to write as bob, use the trick from The Redirect Trap. Check: you and bob can read it, carol cannot; bob cannot write it: he gets the g permissions, r--. → Which Permissions Apply? umask: Predict the permissions of a new file and of a new directory from the umask. print your umask, as a number and as letters; guess the permissions of a new file and of a new directory, then create new.txt and newdir and check. 💡 help umask: search for symbolic. Check: with 0022 (u=rwx,g=rx,o=rx), new.txt is rw-r--r-- and newdir is rwxr-xr-x; with 0002 (Ubuntu), the group also gets w: rw-rw-r-- and rwxrwxr-x. → umask chown: Give a file to another user, and find out who is allowed to do it. give notes.txt to carol, as yourself; do it as root, and list it; give it back to your user and your group, with one command. 💡 man chown: search for colon, to change the group to the login group of the user. Check: as yourself, Operation not permitted; as root, the owner becomes carol; at the end it is yours again. → chown and chgrp Special permissions Special bits on the system: Recognize the special bits on the programs and the directories of the system. print the permissions of /usr/bin/passwd, /usr/bin/su and /usr/bin/sudo, and of the directory /tmp; print them as numbers. Check: the three programs have an s in the place of the x of the owner (4755, and 4111 for sudo on Fedora); /tmp has a t (1777). → Special Permissions The prompt The prompt: Change what the prompt of bash shows, and see that it is only text, which the kernel does not look at. print the value of PS1; change the prompt to student in ~/lab05 $, with the user, the whole path and the $ of the user; add the time in front, as HH:MM; change the prompt so that it looks like the prompt of root; print your user, your UID and the effective user of your shell, and try to print /etc/shadow; go back to the original prompt. 💡 man bash: search for PROMPTING. Check: the original is [\u@\h \W]\$ on Fedora (\u@\h:\w\$ with colors on Ubuntu); the prompt changes right away, and the path changes when you cd. With the fake prompt of root, the user is still student, the UID 1000, and /etc/shadow is still denied: the kernel looks at the credentials, not at the prompt. → The Prompt · Changing the Prompt

Each exercise starts with its goal: what must be true at the end, or what you must find out. The steps lead you there, but you choose the commands.
